States across the nation, including Hawaiʻi, have been integrating nutrition supports into their Medicaid programs 
by using what’s known as the Section 1115 Medicaid Demonstration Waiver.3 4 This five-year waiver allows states to 
test new approaches to delivering and financing Medicaid services that differ from what is normally allowed under 
federal rules. Once approved by the federal government, they allow for innovation within Medicaid, giving sta

fer from what is normally allowed under 
federal rules. Once approved by the federal government, they allow for innovation within Medicaid, giving states 
flexibility to design programs that better meet the specific needs of their population.

Hawaiʻi’s waiver, approved in January 2025, includes the authority to cover the following nutrition support 
services: 1) nutrition education; 2) home-delivered meals or pantry restocking; 3) medically-tailored meals; and 4) 
nutrition prescriptions. More on Hawaiʻi’s 1115 Medicaid waiver can be found in Appendix A.

In alignment with the holistic framing of “food is medicine” described in the introduction, Hawaiʻi is unique 
among other states in its explicit commitment to supporting local farmers and food systems. The waiver states,

“Hawaiʻi will encourage the inclusion of local growers, community gardens, and other 
community-based organizations to support the purchase of locally grown food and 
strengthen Hawaiʻi’s intrinsic food system.” 

— Hawaiʻi Medicaid 1115 Waiver (page 53)

The waiver also notably authorizes the purchase of cooking supplies and supplies to grow fruits and vegetables. 

For this report, Hawaiʻi Appleseed surveyed a range of providers in an attempt to get a broad understanding of 
what is currently available statewide.5 We found that the landscape of nutrition service providers is diverse and 
includes many partners not traditionally involved in modern healthcare operations.

•  Produce prescriptions or protein boxes; 
•  Healthy meals or pantry restocking†; and 
•  Medically-tailored meals or groceries.

Key Findings 

• 

Among organizations surveyed, produce prescriptions or protein boxes were the most popular type of 
nutrition support service, with 21 out of 23 responding organizations stating they either currently offer 
or would like to offer these in the future. However, this service was delivered differently in nearly every 
community surveyed (as seen in the next section on service delivery models). 

•  Nutrition education was the second most popular, and the most widely available currently, with 14 

organizations responding that they currently offer, and another five stating that they would like to offer this 
service in the future. 

• 

Few meal providers participated in the assessment. None of the respondents indicated that they currently 
offer medically tailored meals, although a few organizations do currently offer non-medically tailored meals. 
This may be a sampling error, but could also indicate a capacity gap within Hawaiʻi’s provider network.

 How Are Services Delivered?

In addition to the type of services offered, providers can use a variety of delivery mechanisms to fulfill the 
client's needs. For all the nutrition supports authorized in Hawaiʻi’s 1115 waiver (with the exception of nutrition 
education), clients will receive provisions of food—either meals, groceries, or produce or protein boxes.7 This 
means that, when considering delivery models, organizations have to weigh a variety of factors, including cost, 
availability, storage capacity, perishability, convenience for the client, and the unique needs and assets of the 
organization and community. Flexibility is key, as every community is different. 

Key Findings

•  Hawaiʻi is home to a variety of models, and in some cases, CBOs offer multiple ways to access a particular 

service, as seen in Figure 4.  

•  Providers often use the same terms for different service models. For example, the term “produce 

prescription” can mean a discount code provided to a patient for use at an online food hub, a weekly CSA 
box, a farmer’s market voucher, or some combination of these. 

• 

Service delivery models are not mutually exclusive but generally can be divided by two criteria: 1) custom vs. 
curated, and 2) market pick-up vs. home delivery. Each has its pros and cons, as shown in Figure 5.

Some respondents shared concerns that their ability to plan for the future is limited. A shift toward more

Theme 2: Upfront Investments in CBO Capacity

Hawaiʻi’s waiver authorizes spending up to 15 percent of total health-related social needs expenditures to

partnership requirements.

Recommendation 1: Invest in Community Care Hubs and Network Leads

Providers’ desire for clear guidance is indicative of just how complex providing nutrition support services can

ommunity Care Hubs and Network Leads

Providers’ desire for clear guidance is indicative of just how complex providing nutrition support services can 
be within the managed care landscape. One solution that has proven successful in other states is to build and 
invest in what’s known as Community Care Hubs: entities that centralize administrative functions for a network 
of CBOs, helping them participate in partnerships more effectively.

An important feature of community care hubs (CCHs) is that they understand the values and capacities and have 
trusted relationships with the CBOs they support. 

There is no standard or one-size-fits-all model for a CCH. They may be focused exclusively on one type of service 
(like nutrition supports), a specific type of provider (like community health centers), or a specific geographic 
community. They typically provide the following to their CBO networks: 

•  Backbone Network Support: CCHs create regular and meaningful opportunities for CBOs and providers to 

learn from one another, coordinate on goals, share feedback, and brainstorm solutions. 

•  Direct Administrative Support: They can offer a range of administrative functions, including direct 

contracting with plans, providing patient referrals, or data tracking and reporting. 

•  Training or Technical Assistance: They may provide training or technical assistance for CBOs, or liaise 

between CBOs and MCOs on billing and reimbursement issues.

CBOs and MCOs operate in different spheres and often use distinct language and systems to accomplish

technical assistance marketplace that CBOs can access when challenges arise.

What are Section 1115 Demonstration Waivers?

Medicaid is a joint federal and state program providing health coverage to eligible low-income individuals. The 
program is administered at the state level but follows federal guidelines set by the Centers for Medicare and 
Medicaid Services (CMS)  .

The Medicaid 1115 Demonstration Waiver is an optional five-year waiver that allows states to waive certain 
federal requirements in order to pilot innovative approaches to Medicaid service delivery or financing.24 Most 
projects must be budget-neutral, meaning the federal government's expenditures under the waiver cannot 
exceed what they would have been without the waiver  . An exception is authorized which allows states to spend 
no more than 3 percent of their total state Medicaid spend on health-related social needs (HRSN) and no more 
than 15 percent of their HRSN spending on HRSN-related infrastructure.25

Authorization to Provide Services
Hawai‘i’s Med-QUEST Division requires providers to register using their online HOKU 
enrollment system in order to become authorized for Medicaid reimbursement.

Contracting with Managed Care Organizations
To provide reimbursable services to Medicaid patients, CBOs will need to enter into a 
legally-binding contract with one of the state’s Medicaid managed care plans. Model contracts 
that can be adapted for each partnership are an ideal way to kickstart this process and make it 
feel less daunting.

Screening and Referrals
Our assessment found that many community health centers in Hawai(cid:31)i are already regularly 
screening for food insecurity and other HRSNs. However, those without in-house services will 
need to develop referral systems that can seamlessly connect patients with the appropriate 
services, while also protecting patient privacy. This referral process is typically conducted 
through a HIPAA-compliant electronic health record (EHR) system. 

Reimbursement and Billing Systems
Unlike grant-based funding (which most services in Hawai‘i currently rely on), Medicaid billing, 
reporting, and reimbursement is based on encounters with beneﬁciaries. This transition can be 
one of the biggest challenges for CBOs wishing to provide nutrition and other community 
support services. 

Allowing CBOs to invoice, rather than requiring integrated claims billing, allows partnerships to 
get up and running at early stages, and then move to integrated billing once the partners have 
their balance.

Reporting and Evaluation
CBOs and MCOs often have different deﬁnitions of success. It is crucial to co-develop shared 
goals and metrics that resonate with both parties to ensure effective partnership and shared 
success. This should include metrics that are relevant to the social services provided by CBOs, 
not just health outcomes.

Tax Credits Make Living in Hawai‘i More Affordable

Tax credits are extra money that qualifying people receive when filing their tax returns. They are intended to 
lower the income taxes paid by certain populations, particularly low- to middle-income people. There are two 
major advantages of using tax credits to help people over other types of assistance.

1.  Tax credits are simpler to apply for than government

re two 
major advantages of using tax credits to help people over other types of assistance.

1.  Tax credits are simpler to apply for than government programs. 

If someone meets the basic requirements, they can automatically claim the credit when they file their 
tax return. In comparison, it can take more time and effort to apply for government programs like the 
Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). SNAP recipients have to undergo a lengthy application 
process, which includes an interview, providing documentation, and getting recertified every 6 months. 

2.  Tax credits can be used for any expenses.  

Tax credits can be spent on food, housing, transportation, or anything else that people need in their day-to-
day life. This gives recipients the freedom to decide how they will spend their money, without restrictions. 
On the other hand, SNAP recipients can only spend their benefits on food, excluding hot meals. Likewise, 
housing assistance from the federal government can only be used to pay rent.

 HAWAI‘I’S TAX CREDITS

Although Hawaiʻi has many different tax credits, there is a special category of “social welfare” credits that focus 
on helping low- to middle-income people. Within this category, the four most widely-used tax credits are:

•  The Refundable Food/Excise Tax Credit 

This tax credit was created to offset the impact of the general excise tax (GET), Hawaiʻi’s tax on goods 
and services. Although the GET rais

Credit 

This tax credit was created to offset the impact of the general excise tax (GET), Hawaiʻi’s tax on goods 
and services. Although the GET raises the price of basic necessities for everyone, it affects low-income 
households the most. These households spend a larger portion of their income on basic necessities like 
groceries, which higher-income households can better afford. This Refundable Food/Excise Tax Credit is 
available to individuals earning less than $40,000 and couples earning less than $60,000.10 

•  Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) 

The EITC is intended to benefit low- to middle-income people who are employed, especially if they have 
children. There is a federal EITC that has been in place since 1975, and Hawaiʻi has its own state-level EITC 
that is worth 40 percent of the federal credit. The income limit and credit amount both depend on the 
number of people in a household. In the case of a single parent with three children, the EITC allows for a 
maximum income of $59,899 in tax year 2024.11 The state EITC was also made refundable in 2022, which 
means that low-income households that do not owe much in taxes can still benefit from the credit. 

•  Household and Dependent Care Services Tax Credit (HDCSTC) 

This credit is also known as the Child and Dependent Care Services Tax Credit (CDCTC). It reimburses 
taxpayers for 15 to 25 percent of the cost of providing care to qualifying dependents in their household. 
These “qualifying dependents” are define

s 
taxpayers for 15 to 25 percent of the cost of providing care to qualifying dependents in their household. 
These “qualifying dependents” are defined as children under the age of 13 and individuals who cannot care 
for themselves. There is no income limit, but the credit is capped at $2,500 for one dependent and $5,000 for 
two or more dependents.12 

•  Tax Credit for Low-Income Household Renters 

This tax credit is narrowly targeted at very low-income households that typically do not have enough money 
to pay their rent out-of-pocket. The income limit for this credit is $30,000, and the taxpayer must have 
also paid at least $1,000 in rent for that year to qualify. The credit itself is only worth $50 for each personal 
exemption that the taxpayer can claim for their state income taxes.13 In 2022, this amounted to about $97 on 
average for each taxpayer. Since this credit has not been adjusted for inflation, the number of taxpayers who 
claim it has declined significantly over time. 

The data in the following figures is for the 2022 tax year. Since then, the income limits for the Refundable Food/
Excise Tax Credit have been increased and the tax credit amounts were doubled. In addition, the Household and 
Dependent Care Services Tax Credit has been expanded—though this credit needs to be fixed through additional 
legislation before the changes can actually come into effect.

 THE CHILD TAX CREDIT

First established in 1997, the federal Child Tax Credit (CTC) provides financial relief to families with children—
particularly those with lower incomes. The federal CTC offers a $2,000 credit per child under 18.17 

A temporary increase under the American Rescue Plan (ARP) in 2021 boosted that amount to $3,600 for children 
aged 0–6, and $3,000 for those aged 6–17. In Hawaiʻi, 162,000 families with 272,000 children received the federal 
CTC in 2021.

This expansion significantly reduced child poverty, keeping 2.9 million children out of poverty nationwide, 
especially those from com

especially those from communities of color. However, after the expansion ended, the U.S. poverty rate doubled

Why Hawai‘i Needs Its Own Child Tax Credit

1.  The state does not provide enough tax relief for working families. 

Although Hawaiʻi offers a number of tax credits that assist low-income residents, these credits are too small 
to permanently lift people out of poverty. For example, the Refundable Food/Excise Tax Credit is a great tool 
for helping families offset the regressive GET, but it only gives out an average of $118 to each taxpayer. A 
larger amount of money is needed to get families on their feet in the long term, guaranteeing that they do not 
fall back into financial insecurity. 

2.  Recent tax relief has not targeted those who need it the most. 

House Bill 2404 (2024), which was signed into law by Governor Josh Green in June of 2024, adjusted Hawaiʻi’s 
income tax brackets and standard deduction upward. It will cut income taxes for most people, but high-
income people will ultimately receive the largest benefit. In 2025, the top 1 percent will receive a tax cut of 
more than $6,000, compared to $335 for the bottom 20 percent.19 These changes will also lower Hawaiʻi's tax 
revenue by $1.2 to $1.4 billion by 2031, taking away funds that will be needed to invest in state programs and

These tax credits can be paid for by raising taxes on a small number of wealthy people. There are several ways to 
achieve this, but two that are very good at targeting tax increases only to those who can easily afford to pay are:

ways to

1. Closing the Capital Gains Loophole

Hawaiʻi can better support low-income working families by changing how it taxes income from investments, 
called “capital gains.” Currently, the state taxes capital gains at a lower rate (7.25 percent) than regular income 
(up to 11 percent for the highest earners). This loophole greatly benefits wealthy households that make up a 
large part of their income through investments. In 2025, someone who earns $325,000 from a regular job would 
pay $25,966 in state income taxes. If they earned all of this money through capital gains instead, this person 
would pay a smaller tax of $23,563.

Taxing capital gains at the same rate as regular income could bring in as much as $79 million each year.23 This 
extra money could cover most—if not all—of the funds needed for a state CTC or EITC expansion.

2. Increasing Conveyance Tax Rates on Mansions

Hawaiʻi’s conveyance tax is a fee paid when real estate is sold or transferred. The amount of tax depends on the 
property’s sale price, and whether it will be used as a primary residence. More expensive properties and non-
owner-occupied transactions come with higher tax rates. Some of this revenue flows to the state’s general fund, 
while the remaining portions are set aside for land conservation and affordable housing.

 GLOSSARY OF TERMS

Traffic citation, also colloquially known as a traffic 
ticket, describes the legal document issued by law 
enforcement to a driver for violating traffic laws. 
Citations typically require the recipient to either pay a 
fine, appear in court, or take other specified actions, 
depending on the violation.

Traffic fines and fees describe money-owed for traffic 
citations. While these terms are often lumped together, 
they do have slightly different meanings. Traffic fines 
are monetary penalties imposed for violations of 
traffic laws, while fees are charges that are assessed 
for services related to traffic offenses, such as court 
costs. The key difference is that fines are punitive in 
nature, where fees are typically administrative charges 
associated with handling the violation.

Traffic crime describes serious violations o

ive in 
nature, where fees are typically administrative charges 
associated with handling the violation.

Traffic crime describes serious violations of traffic 
laws that may result in criminal charges, such 
as driving under the influence (DUI) or vehicular 
manslaughter. These offenses often carry more severe 
penalties, such as incarceration, compared to traffic 
infractions. 

Traffic infraction describes a minor violation of traffic 
laws that is typically punishable by a fine rather than 
criminal penalties. 

Traffic violation describes any breach of laws or 
regulations governing vehicle operation on public 
roads. Violations can range from minor infractions 
to serious crimes and may lead to fines, points on a 
driver’s record, or legal repercussions.

Minor or non-serious traffic infractions describe a 
traffic violation that does not impose public safety 
risks, such as a dead taillight or failing to signal. These 
citations usually result in fines but do not typically 
carry criminal charges. 

Criminal-legal system describes the framework 
of laws, institutions, and processes established to 
maintain and enforce laws. It includes law enforcement 
agencies, courts, and correctional facilities. 
Increasingly this term is being used in place of the 
“criminal justice system”, recognizing that instead 
of advancing justice, our current system has harmed 
many communities.

harsh penalties for offenses that pose little risk to the 
public. In this report, Hawaiʻi Appleseed refers to these

advancing transportation equity.

safety. It can also lead to cycles of debt, damaging 
court records and, in some cases, violent interactions 
with police, arrests and incarceration. National data 
shows that communities of color bear the brunt of 
these impacts, particularly violent policing.2

 IMPACTS OF TRAFFIC 
ENFORCEMENT

Driving can have serious consequences for people both inside and outside of vehicles. According to the U.S. 
Department of Transportation, there were more than 42,000 traffic fatalities in the United States in 2022.3 As 
such, all drivers hold an immense responsibility, and serious traffic offenses that have the possibility of causing 
harm—such as speeding and intoxicated driving—warrant some level of enforcement.

However, equitable traffic enforcement requires a clear distinction to be made between serious violations, and 
minor, or non-serious infractions. When used in the report, these terms mean traffic infractions that pose little to 
no threat to public safety. Examples include failing to renew a vehicle registration or crossing the road without 
using a crosswalk. While technically infractions, these behaviors do not significantly endanger other road users. 

In some cases, minor traffic infractions carry heavier penalties than serious traffic violations, and can further 
entrench individuals within cycles of poverty and criminalization. The disconnect between certain traffic laws and 
public safety is exemplified in a statement made by Randy Petersen, a former police officer in Texas, who stated:

 Police Interactions, Pretextual Stops, and Violence

At a minimum, most people experience some form of stress as a result of traffic stops. We heard this countless 
times during our interviews. For example, one interviewee described feeling “vulnerable and powerless” when 
stopped by a police officer for riding a bike on a sidewalk.

However, in some cases, a minor traffic violation can be used by police as an opportunity to investigate more 
serious crimes, such a

on a sidewalk.

However, in some cases, a minor traffic violation can be used by police as an opportunity to investigate more 
serious crimes, such as possession of drugs. This is referred to as a ʻpretextual’ stop. Police often reason that 
pretextual stops are needed to root out more dangerous crime, however, according to one study only 1 percent of 
traffic stops yield a search where contraband is found.5 

Implicit biases can play a large role in pretextual stops. For example, according to one study, Black drivers are 
searched about 1.5 to 2 times as often as white drivers, while they are less likely to be carrying drugs, guns, or 
other illegal contraband, compared to their white peers.6

The consequences of pretextual stops can be profound leading, in some cases, to fines, searches and arrests. 
Moreover, when minor traffic stops lead to more serious situations with police officers, individuals are prone 
to become defensive or anxious. This behavior can be misinterpreted by officers and in some cases, this can 
escalate into confrontations.  

While there are few local examples of pretextual traffic stops turning violent, there are countless national 
examples of high-profile incidents that demonstrate how routine traffic stops can also result in physical 
altercations or, in extreme cases, fatalities. These national incidents also shed light to the fact that communities 
of color have disproportionately borne the brunt of such violence.

Court Records

Because traffic citations are filed by the state court in Hawaiʻi, an individual’s citations record is available 
publicly online via eCourt Kokua.10 Even if the traffic ticket is paid, the citation remains public information unless 
the defendant makes a request to the court to expunge and/or seal the record. Since most minor and non-
serious traffic infractions are considered civil cases, they cannot be expunged from a person’s public record, as 
expungement can only occur for criminal cases. Examples of criminal traffic misdemeanors include intoxicated 
driving, reckless driving

ic record, as 
expungement can only occur for criminal cases. Examples of criminal traffic misdemeanors include intoxicated 
driving, reckless driving, and driving without a license. 

Traffic cases are expunged and/or sealed in Hawaiʻi on a case-by-case basis. Based on information provided 
on the Hawaiʻi Court Records website, requests to seal or expunge traffic cases are typically only granted if the 
case was acquitted, the charges were dismissed, or the conviction was overturned.11 The length of time that 
traffic citations stay on a person’s record vary state by state. Some states allow drivers to attend traffic school in 
exchange for having violations removed from their driving record.

The evergreen nature of traffic court records can have negative implications as sometimes eCourt Kokua is used 
by employers and landlords to conduct background checks on prospective applicants. This can also impact a 
person’s ability to receive affordable car insurance. Many individuals interviewed for this report shared that they 
had paid their traffic citations, primarily so that they would not show up on their record, believing the citations 
would be removed from the public record once the citation had been paid. 

Fines and Debt

Unpaid tickets are typically sent to debt collectors, which can lead to damage to an individual’s credit score. 
Debt collectors can also add collection fees and interest to the original ticket amount, which can make it even 
more challenging to pay th

it score. 
Debt collectors can also add collection fees and interest to the original ticket amount, which can make it even 
more challenging to pay the ticket off. If left unpaid, debt can lead to legal consequences (such as potential court 
appearances and wage garnishment), difficulty in obtaining government services (such as vehicle registration), 
as well as negative impacts to employment and housing opportunities, as some employers and landlords 
conduct credit checks as part of the application process.

Traffic fines can exacerbate economic hardship, pushing families deeper into debt and making it more difficult 
for them to meet basic needs. For example, a 2018 Alabama Appleseed report found that 38 percent of people 
with fines for violations such as low-level vehicle infractions and non-payment of exorbitant court fees ended up 
committing more serious crimes, such as selling drugs, illegal sex work, or robbery, to raise the needed money.12 
This reflects a troubling cycle where minor infractions can escalate into more serious criminal behavior, driven 
by financial desperation.

When a person does not pay their traffic ticket, a “stopper” can be put on a person’s driving or car record, 
which stops the person from obtaining or renewing their license or car registration.13 In 2020, the American Civil 
Liberties Union (ACLU) estimated that a staggering 38 percent of Hawaiʻi drivers (358, 067 people) had a stopper 
on their license or car registration

Liberties Union (ACLU) estimated that a staggering 38 percent of Hawaiʻi drivers (358, 067 people) had a stopper 
on their license or car registration. According to The Washington Post, compared to other states, in 2017 Hawaiʻi 
had among the highest percentage of its over 18 population with suspended license for debt or related reasons.14 

Removing a person’s ability to drive imposes mobility barriers, making it more difficult to access basic services, and

choose to continue to drive, availing themselves to further criminal penalties for driving without a license.

 MINOR VIOLATIONS

Minor Vehicle Violations

The majority of non-serious driving infractions in Hawaiʻi relate to vehicle operation, maintenance and 
compliance. For example, the operation of a vehicle or moped without a certificate of inspection (HRS§286-25) 
can result in a fine of up to $100. Individuals with noisy or altered motorcycle/moped mufflers can receive similar 
penalties. Steeper penalties can occur for driving with tinted windows (HRS§291-21.5), and playing music too 
loudly (HRS§342F-9).  

Penalties increase exponentially when vehicle registration or licensing is involved. While most minor traffic 
violations discussed in this report are categorized as civil traffic violations in Hawaiʻi, the act of driving without a 
license can carry criminal penalties. 

Hawaiʻi has among the strictest laws in the nation for driving without a license, which for a first-time offense 
can include up to 30 days in jail and/or a fine up to $1,000.26 Penalties were also recently increased for multiple 
offenses. Under Act 212 (2024), driving without a valid license can now result in a Class C felony, if the offenses 
occurred within 5 years of each other.27

There are numerous violations in Hawaiʻi that can penalize pedestrians for how, when, and where they cross the

Bicycle Violations

Similar to pedestrians, bicyclists can also be penalized for how they navigate the roadway. For example,

 1. Require Police to Collect Demographic Data

Data collection is an essential tool to understand who is being most impacted by traffic enforcement and to 
combat racial biases in policing. Both at the federal and state level, current data collection of traffic enforcement 
is focused on the number of traffic stops and citations collected. However, this information is limited and does 
not demonstrate whether the enforcement is effective or equitable.32 

Hawaiʻi Appleseed recommends expanded data collection for all traffic stops, including documentation of the 
demographic characteristics of the individual being stopped by the police. At a minimum, this should include the 
person’s self-reported racial and gender identity, as well as their age.

Police Transparency in Washington, D.C.: In 2016, the Council of the District of Columbia passed the 
Neighborhood Engagement Achieves Results Act, which requires Washington, D.C.’s Metropolitan Police 
Department (MPD) to keep extensive records for every stop its officers conduct.33 Notably, for over 3 years, 
the MPD refused to implement this statute until a court ordered compliance as a result of

ry stop its officers conduct.33 Notably, for over 3 years, 
the MPD refused to implement this statute until a court ordered compliance as a result of a lawsuit.34 

The ACLU of Washington, D.C. analyzed police stop data in both 2019 and 2020. In both years the MPD 
disproportionately stopped and searched Black people. For example, in 2020 nearly 75 percent of all 
people stopped by the MPD were Black, while Black people only make up 46 percent of D.C.’s population.35 

According to the National Conference of State Legislators, as of 2021, at least 23 states and D.C. have laws 
regarding the collection of data when an individual is stopped by law enforcement.36

2. Eliminate Unnecessary Pedestrian and Bicycle Enforcement

In Hawaiʻi, pedestrian and bicycle enforcement has not been successful in reducing traffic deaths and injuries, 
and it is clear that business-as-usual will not create safer streets. 

Hawaiʻi Appleseed recommends eliminating unnecessary pedestrian and bicycle enforcement by amending 
HRS§291C to state that pedestrians and bicyclists shall not be stopped by a law enforcement officer, fined, or 
subjected to any other penalty, for acting contrary to the traffic code, so long as they do not pose a threat of a 
collision with another roadway user.

Decriminalizing Jaywalking in California: In 2022, California became the largest state in the nation to 
decriminalize jaywalking. Taking effect on January 1, 2023, the Freedom to Walk Act (AB 2147) prohibits

decriminalize jaywalking. Taking effect on January 1, 2023, the Freedom to Walk Act (AB 2147) prohibits 
pedestrians from being stopped or fined for crossing outside of marked crosswalks, or against a traffic

Although some lawmakers and advocates feared decriminalizing jaywalking would lead to a public safety

3. Reclassify Minor Traffic Violations as Secondary Violations

Enforcement of minor traffic violations can be used as pretextual stops and searches for more serious crimes. At 
a minimum, these stops cause fear and anxiety. In some cases, they can also lead to violent confrontations with 
severe legal consequences. Hawaiʻi Appleseed recommends that the state explore reclassifying certain minor 
traffic violations as secondary

ions with 
severe legal consequences. Hawaiʻi Appleseed recommends that the state explore reclassifying certain minor 
traffic violations as secondary violations. Citations for secondary violations can still be given, however they 
cannot be the sole reason that a person is stopped by the police. 

As an example, if having an expired vehicle registration was reclassified as a secondary violation, police officers 
could not stop an individual solely for that reason. However, if an individual was stopped for another reason—
such as speeding or running a red light—and then was found to also have an expired vehicle registration, then 
they could also be cited for that infraction (in addition to the original violation which the individual was stopped 
for). The collection and reporting of traffic stop data is an important next step to identify which traffic violations 
should be reclassified.

Philadelphia reclassified eight motor vehicle violations—such as late vehicle registration, missing a single 
headlight or taillight, and minor bumper damage—as secondary violations. 

The measure was developed in response to persistent racial disparities in Philadelphia’s traffic

the city’s population.42 In the year following the implementation of the Driving Equality bill, traffic stops 
decreased by 6.8 percent.43 Moreover, during this time period, the proportion of traffic stops made along 
the city’s high injury network increased by 12.3 percent.44 According to the Defender Association of 
Philadelphia, the Driving Equality bill has had no demonstrable negative effect on public safety.45

4. Automatically Seal Traffic Infractions when Cases are Closed

Even after tickets are paid, traffic violations remain on an individual’s public legal record and can pose 
challenges to accessing future insurance, employment, or housing opportunities. Currently, only traffic 
infractions that carry criminal penalties can be expunged and sealed from a person’s record. Hawaiʻi Appleseed 
recommends that the state should automatically seal certain traffic violations. This could be explored as part of 
Hawaiʻi’s Clean Slate Expungement Task Force (enacted via Act 241 in 2024), which is charged with developing a 
state program to proactively expunge certain records of qualified individuals.46 

California’s Clean Slate Laws: Since 2022, the California Department of Justice has been required on 
a monthly basis to review the statewide criminal justice databases and identify persons eligible for 
automatic conviction record relief.47

a monthly basis to review the statewide criminal justice databases and identify persons eligible for 
automatic conviction record relief.47 Eligible individuals include those who were sentenced to probation, 
and completed it without revocation, and those convicted of an infraction or a misdemeanor, including 
traffic infractions. 

Following the passage of Senate Bill 731, which took effect in July 2023, California now automatically seals 
all non-serious, non-violent, and non-sexual felony convictions.48 Generally, convictions are sealed after 4 
years have elapsed since a completed probation or sentence.49 This landmark legislation aimed to alleviate 
the burdens that individuals with criminal-legal records face, and has provided inspiration for similar 
clean slate efforts in Hawaiʻi and elsewhere.

5. Build Unarmed Traffic Enforcement Teams

The presence of law enforcement can create stressful, hostile environments, and in some rare cases, can escalate 
into violent encounters. The enforcement of most traffic violations, particularly minor traffic violations, does not 
require armed police. Hawaiʻi Appleseed recommends that local law enforcement agencies build unarmed teams 
to carry out enforcement of minor traffic violations.

Berkley to De-Cop its Traffic Enforcement: Berkeley, California, is poised to become the first city 
in the U.S. to replace police officers with unarmed employees to carry out a majority of its

Berkeley, California, is poised to become the first city 
in the U.S. to replace police officers with unarmed employees to carry out a majority of its traffic 
enforcement.50 The proposal, approved in 2020, sought to create a separate department for unarmed 
public works officials to carry out traffic enforcement.51 

While the Berkeley City Council approved a budget in 2022 that would include funding for the department, 
it has yet to be implemented. According to the Stanford Center for Racial Justice, police opposition is a 
major reason for slow implementation.52

6. Create an Income-Based Traffic Fines System

The current system of flat fees for traffic violations disproportionately burdens low-income individuals, 
worsening existing inequalities and perpetuating cycles of poverty. A single traffic ticket can impose significant 
financial strain on those who are already struggling to make ends meet, often leading to a cascade of missed 
payments and debt. Notably, while most criminal legal fees in Hawaiʻi offer an “ability to pay” option, it remains 
at the judge’s discretion whether to grant it or not. It is also unclear how often this option is implemented. 

Hawaiʻi Appleseed recommends exploring the implementation of a traffic fines and fees system based on 
income, instead of using flat fees. This means that wealthier individuals pay more for the same violation than 
those with lower incomes. This not only ensures that penalties are equitable, but also maintains comp

Finland’s Day Fines System: In Finland, like other Scandinavian and European countries, fines for traffic 
violations are based on an individual’s daily income, as well as the severity of the violation. This system, 
known as a “day fines” system, was first created in Finland in the 1920s. When issuing traffic tickets, police 
have access to a central taxpayer database to determine the person’s daily income.53 

While Finland has made national headlines for its wealthy elites racking up exorbitantly high fines, these 
instances are rare. Over the last century, the day fines system has been effective in deterring traffic 
violations without burdening lower-income drivers. 

Based on 2021 data from the World Health Organization, Finland has one of the lowest road fatality rates 
in the world, with only 4.2 annual traffic deaths per 1,000 people.54 Comparatively, there are 14.1 annual 
traffic deaths per 1,000 people in the United States.55

Renters in Hawaiʻi face significant cost burdens and limited protection from displacement. Hawaiʻi 
renters are often evicted or forced to self-evict under a range of circumstances.6

A National Low Income Housing Coalition (NLIHC) snapshot of the cost of renting in Hawaiʻi done in 
2023 shows that 38 percent of residents are renters, with 21 percent earning low incomes and 36 percent 
earning extremely low-incomes.7 More than half (51 percent) of all renters now spend more than 30 
percent of their income on rent, making them “cost-burdened.” Furthermore, 26 percent of all renters are 
“severely cost burdened,” which means they spend more than 50 percent of their income on rent.8

Displacement and housing instability have profound consequences for individuals and families beyond 
the obvious financial burden. Studies show that housing instability is also linked to increased stress, 
anxiety, and depression, all of which can deteriorate both mental and physical well-being.9 Chronic

For children, housing instability can also lead to interruptions in education, with frequent moves

Hawaiʻi’s high housing costs and comparatively low wages, coupled with low levels of protection 
for renters, has left a very large portion of our residents vulnerable to displacement and the social

Impacts of the Maui Wildfires

In addition to the tragic loss of more than 100 lives, the Maui Wildfires devastated 2,207 
structures. Some 86 percent of these structures were residential, including an 89 unit affordable 
rental housing project that Hawaiʻi Appleseed worked with residents and local attorneys to 
keep affordable.15 Prior to the 2023 Maui Wildfires, Hawaiʻi was already the 4th most expensive 
state for renters.16 The loss of these housing units displaced thousands of Lahaina residents and 
exacerbated an already dire

he 4th most expensive 
state for renters.16 The loss of these housing units displaced thousands of Lahaina residents and 
exacerbated an already dire situation for Maui County.

In the aftermath of the fires, policies designed to rehouse displaced residents led to 
unintended consequences.17 The Federal Emergency Management Agency’s generous rental 
assistance—$5,000 per studio unit and up to $11,000 a month for a four-bedroom18—doubled the 
market rate for most rental units.19 This pushed the rental market beyond the reach of current 
residents across the county, forcing them to either leave their homes or pay exorbitant new 
market prices.20

While the aid benefited those directly affected by the fires, renters who were not directly 
impacted now face an increased risk of displacement.21 The vulnerability of Maui County’s 
struggling, wider renter population underscores the urgent need for legislative intervention to 
protect renters and ensure the availability of affordable housing options. Without a significant 
increase in housing units and improvements in housing affordability, the housing market will 
continue to exclude working-class people across Hawaiʻi.

During the 2024 legislative session, members of the Maui delegation introduced numerous 
bills aimed at regulating the rental market, including proposals for rent price restrictions and 
mediation requirements.

The landlord-tenant law in the Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes is limited in protections against displacement. 
Enforcement of the landlord-tenant code favors landlords implicitly by not providing tenants with a 
guaranteed right to counsel. Rental assistance is limited and can’t always cover the necessary funds to 
bridge a gap in rent owed versus cash available. 

The majority of Hawaiʻi’s rental assistance programs in existence today feature a number of barriers 
tenants must overcome, have a long waiting period, or require showing that the tenant is homeless or 
about to become homeless to qualify. With just a five-day eviction notice required for non-payment of 
rent, there is almost no time for renters to access, or qualify for temporary assistance.

Best Practices for Tenant Protections

The NLIHC has published multiple reports on efforts to further increase the security of renters. 
Lack of federal tenant protections means that states must legislate these protections to avoid 
harmful power imbalances between landlords and tenants. In the “State of Statewide Renter 
Protections” (2023), the NLIHC found that across the U.S. there are five common types of state-
level protections to support housing stability and prevent harmful evictions:

1.  Right to Counsel: Ensures that tenants facing eviction are guaranteed legal representation in 
court, helping to prevent unjust evictions and ensuring fair legal proceedings for renters who 
cannot afford an attorney. 

2.  Just Cause Eviction: Mandates that landlords can only evict tenants for specific, 

documented reasons (such as non-payment of rent or lease violations), rather than at the 
landlord’s discretion. This offers greater protection against capricious displacement. 

3.  Source of Income Discrimination: Prohibits landlords from refusing to rent to potential 

tenants based on their source of income, such as relying on government subsidies or housing 
vouchers. This ensures equitable access to housing for low-income individuals. 

4.  Eviction Record Sealing and Ex

n government subsidies or housing 
vouchers. This ensures equitable access to housing for low-income individuals. 

4.  Eviction Record Sealing and Expungement Laws: Allow individuals with eviction records to 
have their records sealed or expunged after a certain period, providing a second chance and 
helping to reduce barriers to securing future housing. 

5.  Anti-Rent Gouging: Imposes restrictions on how much landlords can increase rent, 

particularly during emergencies or periods of high demand, to protect tenants from excessive 
rent hikes.

Hawaiʻi currently has in effect a source of income discrimination law on the books. However,  it 
exempts property owners who own less than four units, making it overly narrow in scope.

 RECOMMENDATIONS

Hawaiʻi's existing statutes do not provide sufficient protection against displacement. There are no just-
cause eviction requirements, little if any rental support, no advance notice of lease non-renewal or rent 
increases, and no accessible resources for mediating landlord-tenant disputes. Furthermore, there is 
no effective enforcement mechanism for violations of the landlord-tenant code. The absence of a right 
to counsel exacerbates these issues. Tenants without legal representation face significant challenges in 
contesting illegal evictions or displacement. 

Hawaiʻi needs a comprehensive revision of its landlord-t

epresentation face significant challenges in 
contesting illegal evictions or displacement. 

Hawaiʻi needs a comprehensive revision of its landlord-tenant code. A robust renters' rights policy is 
essential for ensuring tenants live in safe, fair, and secure housing. Such a policy should include:

1.  Access to Legal Resources: Information and support for tenants to understand and be able to 

exercise their rights. 

2.  Protection Against Unlawful Eviction: Legal processes for evictions, protection against retaliatory 

actions, and access to contest eviction notices. 

3.  Transparent and Fair Leasing Practices: Clear lease agreements, fair rent increase regulations, and 

procedures for lease termination. 

4.  Privacy and Respect: Reasonable notice before landlord entry and prohibition of harassment. 

5.  Fair Rent Practices: Regulated rent increases and clear communication of changes. 

6.  Security Deposits: Fair handling of deposits, including clear procedures for interest, deductions, as 

well as returns. 

7.  Non-Discrimination: Enforcement of anti-discrimination laws in rental practices. 

8.  Support for Vulnerable Populations: Additional protections for low-income renters, seniors, and 

individuals with disabilities. 

9.  Right to Safe and Habitable Housing: Ensuring properties meet health and safety standards, with 

mandatory repairs and inspections.

 RECOMMENDATIONS

Just Cause: The policy should require that documented just cause be required for evictions. Just cause 
should include: non payment of rent, substantial damage to the premises, threatening injury or injuring 
others on premise, reckless endangerments, material violation of lease, repeat violation after receipt 
of proper notice of violation, nuisance disturbance or negligent damage to property, property damage, 
failure to disclose sex offender status, sexual advances or harassment of owner or manager or other 
tenants, and threats to landlord. 

No Fault Cause: The policy should provide that tenants cannot be held at fault in the event of demolition 
or conversion of residential premises, substantial repair or renovation, documented need for landlord 
or landlord’s family member to assume occupancy, selling of home, notice of non renewal of lease by 
landlord under 90 days, or notice of rental increase under 60 days. 

Relocation Assistance: In the event of demolition or conversion of residential premises, the policy 
should require relocation assistance to supplement renters previous housing costs u

t of demolition or conversion of residential premises, the policy 
should require relocation assistance to supplement renters previous housing costs up to six months, and 
for all other no fault cause one month’s rent for relocation assistance or waiver of the final month of rent.

Enforcement: Effective enforcement of these protections ensures that these policies are actively 
implemented, preventing exploitation and further displacement. Enforcement mechanisms should 
include regular inspections, clear reporting procedures, and accessible legal support.

Right To Counsel: When facing eviction, just 4 percent of tenants are represented by counsel as opposed 
to 83 percent of landlords. Across the country there are approximately 24 jurisdictions that have enacted 
tenant right-to-counsel measures, with reported positive outcomes that maintain tenant occupancy and 
limit no-fault evictions. 

In Oklahoma, Massachusetts, California, Minnesota and Denver, Colorado, studies consistently show 
that tenants with legal counsel are significantly more likely to retain their housing or receive more time 
to find alternative accommodations. Specifically, legal representation increases the odds of staying in 
a home by up to 75 percent, with some studies revealing that fully represented tenants are three times 
more likely to stay in their units, and therefore avoid homelessness. Additionally, tenants with counsel 
tend to have cleaner eviction records, which can help avoid future housin

units, and therefore avoid homelessness. Additionally, tenants with counsel 
tend to have cleaner eviction records, which can help avoid future housing instability.23 

These findings underscore the need for a right to legal representation in eviction proceedings, as it 
ensures tenants have a fair opportunity to remain in their homes, access sufficient time to relocate, and 
avoid the long-term negative consequences of eviction. Providing legal assistance to tenants can prevent 
displacement, reduce homelessness and promote housing stability. 

Hawaiʻi can create a more equitable rental market, ensuring that all residents—particularly those most 
in need—have access to safe and affordable housing. Addressing these gaps will not only support renters 
but also contribute to a more stable housing market overall, benefiting the community as a whole.

The 2025 legislative session offers another opportunity to pass sensible landlord-tenant code reform 
around just cause eviction, right to counsel, and extended notice. Without comprehensive reforms, we 
risk further social and economic disruptions, along with enduring health consequences for Hawaiʻi’s 
most vulnerable populations.

 Obligated Costs

Before the state can consider any other spending, the Hawaiʻi constitution says it must pay its 
non-negotiable obligated costs. These costs include pensions, health benefits, Medicaid, and debt 
payments—and they are worth $5 billion, or a quarter of the state’s operating budget. The share of the 
operating budget that these costs consume is increasing each year, limiting the state’s flexibility for new 
investments in areas like housing, schools, economic development and climate resilience.

Except for Medicaid expenses, which are included in the budget for the Department of Human Services, 
the costs named above are covered by the Department of Budget and Finance. These two departments 
have the largest operating budgets, and obligated costs are a significant share for each.

In Hawaiʻi, low- and middle-income families spend a larger share of their already stretched-thin income on state 
and local taxes compared to wealthy families. This is due almost entirely to the General Excise Tax, which is 
charged on basic needs like food, clothes and rent. When a low-income person and a wealthy person purchase the 
same groceries, they pay the same dollar amount of tax. However, that dollar amount represents a much larger 
chunk of the low-income person’s paycheck, making it much harder to budget for—and too often keeping low-
income families trapped in cycles of poverty, debt and income insecurity.

Tax Credits

Tax credits are an effective tool available to lawmakers that are designed to lower or even eliminate the

hunger and poor nutrition for many families.

•  Nearly 1 in 3 Hawaiʻi households struggle with food insecurity.11 Among food insecure households with keiki,

These figures are staggering, and dramatically underscore the harmful impacts of colonialism on native food

Hawaiʻi has lost millions of dollars in federal emergency food assistance funding.14 Looming federal SNAP cuts are

Equitable access to transportation—and the mobility that comes with it—is more than a question of convenience. 
It is a fundamental need for survival. However, our current transportation system does not provide equitable 
access to mobility.

•  Our transportation system is heavily reliant on vehicle travel, and fails to deliver equitable access to those who 
do not drive. This system creates unsustainable levels of traffic, negatively impacting the health and quality of 
life of residents, and contributing heavily to climate degradation.15 Often it is the most vulnerable who pay the 
heaviest price for this flawed system, including keiki, kūpuna and rural residents. 

• 

In rural Hawaiʻi County, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders are 300 percent more likely to die in vehicle 
collisions compared to the state average.16 Honolulu’s densely-populated, urban areas, with large mixed-Asian, 
Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Island populations, are hotspots for jaywalking citations compared to lower-
density, higher income suburban areas with larger Asian and White populations.17

 HOW PARKING IMPACTS 
AFFORDABLE HOUSING

Parking mandates significantly influence the affordability and design of housing developments. When mandated 
by local ordinance or included voluntarily by developers, the addition of parking spaces directly affects 
construction cost and housing prices. 

The construction of parking spaces is an expensive undertaking, with costs varying based on the type and location 
of the parking (including surface, podium and underground). A 2020 study from the Ulupono Initiative highlights 
just how prohibitively expensive parking is. According to the study, the cost to build parking in low- and mid-rise 
multifamily buildings (with surface parking) adds between $5,000 and $35,000 per affordable rental unit, and 
between $5,000 and $45,000 per for-sale unit.2

The costs of parking are highest on Oʻahu, where the majority of Hawaiʻi’s residents

ental unit, and 
between $5,000 and $45,000 per for-sale unit.2

The costs of parking are highest on Oʻahu, where the majority of Hawaiʻi’s residents live. In high-rise residential 
developments in Honolulu’s urban core that include podium parking, the added cost of parking in 2020 was 
estimated at $55,000 per housing unit for affordable and mixed-income rentals.3 Adjusted for inflation, this cost 
now exceeds $68,000 per unit. 

“WE HAVE EXPENSIVE HOUSING FOR PEOPLE AND FREE 

PARKING FOR CARS.” 

—Donald Shoup, author of The High Cost of Free Parking 

Affordable housing developments operate on tight margins. The added expense of parking can reduce the number 
of units that developers are able to deliver, or make projects financially infeasible altogether. For example, 
imagine a high-rise building with 200 mixed-income rental units and podium parking is planned in Honolulu. If 
one parking stall is built for every two units, this would add $6.8 million to the cost of the project in 2025 dollars. 

The cost of building parking is usually passed on to the residents, either through higher rents or purchase prices.
For a single person renting a small studio in urban Honolulu, parking could add up $410 per month to their rent—
even if they don’t own a vehicle.4

Parking does not only increase the cost of development. It also affects the design of housing and the built 
environment. For example, parking mandates make it harder to build smaller, space-efficient housing such as

environment. For example, parking mandates make it harder to build smaller, space-efficient housing such as 
townhomes and accessory dwelling units, especially on narrow lots or in dense neighborhoods. As a result, these 
mandates discourage the development of smaller, more affordable housing options. Parking mandates can also

The prioritization of parking forces developers to sacrifice housing opportunities for car storage. This trade-off 
becomes particularly stark in urban environments where land is limited and housing demand is high. The land 
required to accommodate surface parking could instead be used to construct additional housing units, community 
amenities, or green spaces. 

Parking-dedicated spaces also limit opportunities for active ground-floor uses such as retail or community 
facilities, diminishing a neighborhood’s vibrancy and walkability. As such, parking mandates create auto-centric 
environments and limit residents’ mobility options (Figure 1). By prioritizing parking mandates, we effectively 
choose to allocate land—a finite and valuable resource—to cars, rather than to people.

 EFFORTS TO REDUCE 
PARKING MANDATES

Across the United States, communities are eliminating costly parking mandates. As of 2025, 93 cities in the United 
States have removed all their jurisdiction’s parking mandates, with 75 of them within the past five years alone.6 

• 

• 

In Birmingham, Alabama officials have taken these steps to lower development costs and respond to rising 
living expenses, noting that old zoning laws ignored the realities of many residents who lack reliable car 
access. Recent record-breaking heat has driven the city to reduce paved surfaces and expand green space.7 

In Washington County, Oregon officials adopted reforms under the state’s Climate-Friendly and Equitable 
Communities initiative, pairing the removal of parking mandates with tree canopy requirements for large lots.8

•  Gilman, Wisconsin—a town of less than 500 people—has had no off-street parking mandates since 2011.9

1. Implement Parking Maximums in TOD Areas

To complement the reduction of parking mandates, TOD areas should implement parking maximums for 
residential projects—setting a firm cap on the number of parking spaces per dwelling unit. 

Parking maximums were considered during the crafting of Ordinance 20-41. The findings in this study confirm the 
need for them: Despite the elimination of mandates, for-sale housing developers continue to over-build parking in 
well-served transit areas.

OVER THE PAST SEVERAL DECADES, the United States has experienced a dramatic rise in the frequency, severity, 
and geographic reach of climate-driven disasters—from hurricanes and floods, to wildfires and extreme heat.

These tragic events devastate communities and take lives. They also strain the financial infrastructure that 
underpins recovery: the property insurance system.

As disaster claims mount, private insurers are taking in record profits while adopting strategies that harm 
consumers. These tactics include pleading depletion of ca

ms mount, private insurers are taking in record profits while adopting strategies that harm 
consumers. These tactics include pleading depletion of capital reserves despite record CEO pay,1 retreating from 
high-risk markets, or sharply increasing premiums. 

In a self-reinforcing cycle, these firms then reinvest their profits into the very fossil fuel companies that intensify the 
climate disasters that force them to abandon vulnerable markets.2

In the wake of this abandonment, federal and state governments have been forced to intervene with a patchwork 

CLIMATE DISASTERS • 3

 of strategies, ranging from legislative reforms and public “insurers of last resort,” to expansion of programs like 
the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). 

At the same time, legal doctrines such as subrogation, shifting norms in public-private responsibility, and the 
growing role of catastrophe modeling are redefining how insurance works in the age of accelerating climate change. 

These pressures are more acute in Hawaiʻi: over 60 percent of our housing stock was constructed before 1990. This 
aging housing stock carries added risk, and requires regular maintenance and costly resilience upgrades. These 
are major financial barriers for many in a state with some of the highest housing costs in the U.S.3 

Additionally, 40 percent of Hawaiʻi’s available housing stock is in multifamily buildings, structures that require 
property insurance not just as a financial safeguard, but as a precondit

available housing stock is in multifamily buildings, structures that require 
property insurance not just as a financial safeguard, but as a precondition for mobility, homeownership and 
equity. Without insurance, rents increase, mortgages collapse, units become unsellable, and entire condominium 
associations can be left exposed to catastrophic risk.

Two major sets of factors interact to drive instability in Hawaiʻi’s insurance sector: 

•  Property-specific issues, such as building age, deferred maintenance and loss history; and 

• 

Systemic dynamics, such as global reinsurance markets, catastrophe risk and regulatory constraints. 

Between 2018 and 2023, nonrenewals for insurance policies increased by nearly 216 percent across the state.4 
Between 2021 to 2024, Hawaiʻi homeowners saw an average increase in insurance premiums of 12 percent,5 and 
condo Home Owners Associations have seen an average increase of 16 percent, with fee increases ranging from $1 
to more than $2,000.6

This report investigates how climate change is reshaping the structure, function and equity of insurance markets—
nationally and in Hawaiʻi. It explores:

•

The historical interaction between climate disasters, market retrenchment and government intervention;

The particular vulnerabilities facing Hawaiʻi’s housing insurance system;

The legal, regulatory, and market tools being mobilized to manage escalating risk; and

By analyzing both past disasters and unfolding crises, the report captures a system in flux—where each disaster 
reshapes not only the built environment but also the financial rules, legal responsibilities, and social norms that 
determine who is protected, who pays for recovery, and who is left behind. 

To build a more resilient and equitable future for Hawaiʻi’s residents, this report recommends: 

1.  Enabling the state to subrogate companies most responsible for climate disasters; 

2.  Reshaping land use patterns to create natural resiliency buffers; 

3.  Retrofitting older housing stock to withstand climate impacts; 

4.  Adopting and enforcing updated building codes for new construction; and 

5.  Expanding education on risk management and available resources to help households and communities take 

preventative measures.

 GLOSSARY OF TERMS

•  Catastrophic risk: Low-frequency, high-severity risk that can cause large, simultaneous losses across 
many policyholders, often overwhelming the financial capacity of insurers. Catastrophic risks—such 
as major hurricanes, wildfires, earthquakes, or other climate-driven disasters—are difficult to diversify 
and often require reinsurance, public backstops, or government intervention to manage.

• 

• 

• 

Insurability: The extent to which

lt to diversify 
and often require reinsurance, public backstops, or government intervention to manage.

•

Insurability: The extent to which a risk can be covered by an insurer at a reasonable price and under 
workable conditions. A risk is considered insurable when losses are predictable enough to price, 
not excessively likely or severe, and can be spread across a broad pool. As climate-driven disasters 
become more frequent and severe, some areas and properties may become less insurable, even if 
insurance products still technically exist.

Insurance: A financial arrangement in which individuals or organizations transfer risk to an insurer 
in exchange for paying premiums. Insurance works by pooling risks across many policyholders, 
allowing the costs of losses to be shared.

Insurer of last resort: A government-run or government-backed insurance entity that provides 
coverage where private insurers will not, typically because the risk is considered too high, 
unpredictable, or unprofitable. These programs act as a safety net to ensure that people and 
communities can still obtain essential insurance in areas facing catastrophic or concentrated risks, 
such as hurricanes, wildfires, floods, or volcanic eruptions. 

•  Moral hazard: A situation in which individuals or organizations change their behavior because they 
are insulated from the consequences of risk, often due to insurance coverage or public support. In 
climate-related disasters, moral hazard may occur

are insulated from the consequences of risk, often due to insurance coverage or public support. In 
climate-related disasters, moral hazard may occur when properties continue to be built or rebuilt in 
high-risk areas because insurance, subsidies, or public aid reduce the perceived cost of exposure.

•  Prior approval (insurance rate regulation): A state regulatory process that requires insurance 
companies to submit proposed rates for review and obtain approval from the state insurance 
regulator before the rates can be used. Prior approval is designed to ensure that rates are not 
excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory, especially in markets affected by rising climate-
related risks. 

•  Reinsurance: Insurance that insurance companies purchase to protect themselves against very large 

or catastrophic losses.

•  Subrogation: The legal process that allows an insurer to seek reimbursement from a third party that 
caused the loss after the insurer has paid a claim to the policyholder. Subrogation shifts costs back to 
the party responsible for the damage, helping to reduce overall losses in the insurance system.

 ISSUE OVERVIEW

Property insurance is not just a financial safeguard—it also functions as a gatekeeper to the U.S. housing system. 
Access to coverage determines access to mortgage finance and, without that, homes become uninsurable, 
unsellable and ultimately inaccessible. This dynamic is especially acute in multifamily housing m

inance and, without that, homes become uninsurable, 
unsellable and ultimately inaccessible. This dynamic is especially acute in multifamily housing markets such as 
Hawaiʻi, where approximately 40 percent of the existing housing stock is multifamily.7

Nationally, climate change is destabilizing insurance markets through cascading effects on affordability and 
availability. Between 2020 and 2023, average homeowners insurance premiums rose by about 30 percent.8 At the 
same time, the costs of home repair climbed by more than 50 percent in just two years, further amplifying insurer 
exposure.9 These pressures have led private insurers to retreat from an increasing number of high-risk markets, 
leaving entire regions with limited or no access to new coverage.10

In California, the top three insurers stopped writing new homeowners policies in wildfire-prone zones.11 In 2023 
alone, State Farm declined to renew over 70,000 policies.12 

Florida’s state-backed insurer of last resort, Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, has ballooned to more 
than 1.4 million policies, making it one of the 10 largest insurers in the nation.13 Such programs are designed as 
temporary backstops, but Florida’s program now shoulders systemic levels of risk.

The Urban Climate Change Research Network has described this convergence of climate pressures, market

threatens to make housing financially inaccessible to tens of millions of people, undermining not only property

 CASE STUDIES

Case studies provide a critical window into how legislatures respond when natural disasters threaten the viability 
of home insurance markets. Each event forces policymakers to confront the same dilemma: how to stabilize 
insurance availability without undermining affordability or driving private carriers out of the market. 

By examining the tools deployed in different contexts—from the creation of state-run insurers of last resort, to 
reforms in catastrophe modeling, to federal interventions through programs like the National Flood Insurance 
Plan (NFIP)—we can trace how regulatory choices shape long-term outcomes for homeowners. Looking at these 
responses side by side not only reveals the diversity of strategies, but also highlights their lasting implications for 
equity, access to credit, and the overall resilience of housing systems.

When Hurricane Andrew struck South Florida in August 1992, it left behind one of the costliest natural disasters

Climate risk is not evenly distributed across 
Hawaiʻi’s islands. Current development patterns have allowed for housing to be built in some of our most 
vulnerable zones: low-lying coastal areas threatened by sea level rise and flooding, or fire-prone landscapes at 
the urban-wildland boundary.106 Continuing to approve the same land use patterns in these areas compounds 
exposure and ultimately shifts escalating insurance and recovery costs on to households and the public.107

Other states are proactively confronting climate risk in land use planning by establishing new policies that directly 
link zoning, infrastructure and hazard reduction. South Carolina mandates a “resiliency element" in all local 
comprehensive plans, so cities and counties must systematically evaluate and address vulnerabilities to flooding, 
sea level rise, and other hazards.108

Similarly, New Jersey and Washington state have made climate hazard assessments a requirement for local 
planning, tying them directly to decisions about new development, infrastructure investments, and zoning 
changes to minimize future disaster exposure.109 Even the federal NFIP incentivizes smarter land use by rewarding 
jurisdictions that adopt floodplain management and mitigation strategies with lower insurance premiums for local 
residents through a Community Rating System (CRS).110

This concept isn’t foreign to Hawaiʻi. After a tsunami devastated Hilo town in 1946 and killed 159 people, the 
community rebuilt on the same spot only to suffer the same devastating consequences in 1960 after another 
tsunami struck.111 

The response to the 1960 tsunami was dramatically different. Hawaiʻi County undertook major changes to land 
use, hazard planning, and disaster resilience to protect the vulnerable coastal city.112 The county government 
mandated a broader oceanside greenbelt bufferzone of lagoons, gardens, and recreational facilities designed to 
protect inland areas by absorbing the impacts of future tsunamis.113

Resilient land use planning gives local governments a powerful tool to contain risk, reduce potential of moral 
hazards, and promote both safety and equity.114 By strengthening zoning and hazard mitigation policies, Hawaiʻi 
can help stabilize insurance markets, relieve low- and moderate-income households of hidden financial burdens, 
and turn smart land use into a foundation for long-term disaster resilience.

 NEW HOUSING: BUILT FOR RESILIENCE

Over 60 percent of Hawaiʻi’s housing stock was built before 1990. That means the majority of our housing is 30 
years or older. During a three decade time span, roofs should be replaced, pipes checked and updated, and retrofit 
requirements for single-wall homes or sprinkler upgrades for condos should be completed at least once. That 
includes hurricane clips115—metal

trofit 
requirements for single-wall homes or sprinkler upgrades for condos should be completed at least once. That 
includes hurricane clips115—metal connectors that reinforce the connection between a home’s roof and walls. 
These are all expensive upgrades and retrofits to make for older housing stock. 

The Marco Polo residential building in Honolulu was required to retrofit 568 units after a 2017 fire, the cost of 
which was nearly $9,000 per unit for an overall $5 million upgrade.116 To add hurricane clips to single family 
homes, prices start around $1,500 and go up depending on construction type and number of stories.117 For many 
residents, these kinds of expenses are simply not feasible.118 119 

Environmental conditions in Hawaiʻi accelerate deterioration. Termites, mold, sun, saltwater, and humidity all 
shorten the lifespan of building materials.120 The result is that much of our older housing stock has not kept 
up with evolving safety requirements or higher standards demanded by insurers. Many properties face rising 
premiums, non renewals, or limited coverage—not because residents have done anything wrong, but because the 
buildings themselves are aging out of compliance.

Facing a dual challenge, Hawaiʻi must retrofit its older housing for climate resilience—a costly but essential task—
while ensuring new construction meets modern codes from the start. Strengthening existing homes protects 
current communities and affordability, while building resilient new ho

current communities and affordability, while building resilient new housing secures a safer, more insurable future 
for all.

Actionable tools that the state and counties can use to build resilient communities, upgrade both older and newer 
housing stock, and address moral hazard in insurance markets include:

•  Code Updates and Resilience Overlays. Fast-track adoption of the latest hazard-specific building codes, 

moving urgently from 2018 codes to current international standards and tailor amendments for regional risks 
such as hurricanes, wildfires and coastal flooding.121  

Develop overlay zones within local zoning maps, applying stricter resilience standards, including elevation, 
fire resistance and hurricane protection in areas with the highest environmental risk.122

•  Retrofit Incentive Programs & Anti-Displacement Provisions. Expand state and county tax credits 

specifically for upgrades like hurricane clips, fire-resistant roofing, elevation, and pest/moisture mitigation.  

Establish and fully fund grants or low-interest loans for multifamily properties to facilitate sprinkler retrofits, 
resilient utility upgrades, climate-proof heating/cooling, and full roof and plumbing replacements.  

Pair incentives with robust anti-displacement protections, such as requiring tenant habitability plans, 
temporary relocation assistance, and rent stabilization during retrofit work.

 INTRODUCTION: 
WHY COUNTY 
ACTION MATTERS

COUNTIES HAVE A CRITICAL ROLE to play in strengthening food security, especially as Hawaiʻi faces rising costs 
of living and high rates of food insecurity. 

According to recent numbers, food insecurity is a pressing challenge across the islands: Hawaiʻi Island faces the 
greatest impact, where 43 percent of households are affected. Sizeable proportions in Maui (41 percent), Kauaʻi 
(32 percent), and Oʻahu (25 percent) also report difficulty accessing enough food.1 

At the same time, shifting federal priorities and proposed cuts to nutrition and health programs threaten to 
reduce the reliability of resources that low-income families rely on, including the Supplemental Nutrition 
Assistance Program (SNAP) and Medicaid.

Since 2018, each county has added a dedicated Food Access Co

s rely on, including the Supplemental Nutrition 
Assistance Program (SNAP) and Medicaid.

Since 2018, each county has added a dedicated Food Access Coordinator (FAC), partially funded by the SNAP-
Education program and administered through the Hawaiʻi Department of Health.2 These FACs play a central 
role in assessing community needs, leading the development of county-wide Food Systems Plans, and 
mapping emergency food-response efforts.3 In 2025, Congress cut SNAP-Ed funding with the passage of H.R.1. 
Without stable funding for these critical positions, communities risk losing the backbone of their local food 
security infrastructure.

Against this backdrop, counties are uniquely positioned to adapt and respond to smaller-scale community 
needs. Unlike federal and state programs, county-level governance has a closer connection to residents, making 
for community-focused solutions that reflect local needs. 

For instance, as the state’s most rural county,4 Hawaiʻi County’s approach to food production may reflect its 
uniquely dispersed communities and agricultural landscape. Maui County, on the other hand, is the only county 
comprising three islands, and may need to prioritize interisland transportation support for Molokaʻi and Lanaʻi to 
address geographic barriers to access. 

While this report aims to evaluate the current programs and resources that counties in Hawaiʻi can use to 
strengthen food security, these recommendations are not meant as a replacement of entire nu

rograms and resources that counties in Hawaiʻi can use to 
strengthen food security, these recommendations are not meant as a replacement of entire nutrition programs 
like SNAP, which are seeing historically drastic reductions in benefits and overall funding. Nor do these 
recommendations assume that counties will be shouldering these efforts alone. County efforts must be coupled 
with significant state support, and utilization of federal programs that remain strong.

Rationale: Summer meal programs provide a critical bridge by ensuring children continue to receive the nutrition

Across Hawaiʻi, Departments of Parks and Recreation (DPRs) in every county have, at one point, sponsored the

Key Agency: Varies

Rationale: Food banks play a critical role, especially for people who don’t qualify for other types of food 
assistance. They are often seen as a “last line of defense” for families when no other options are available. While 
federal programs often provide a baseline of support, these charitable organizations tend to rely largely on 
donations.29 Funding from both the state and county can enable a more flexible response to the steadily increasing 
need that food banks are seeing as food costs rise.

Although it is not yet common in Hawaiʻi, counties can directly support these critical institutions, tailoring 
programs to each county’s need. County funds can be targeted to help expand food distribution, purchase fresh or 
culturally relevant foods, support local farmers, and strengthen infrastructure like cold storage and transportation.

 CONCLUSION

Counties across Hawaiʻi face both pressing challenges and powerful opportunities in the fight against food 
insecurity. With federal nutrition programs under threat and state resources stretched thin, counties cannot afford 
to remain passive. By implementing existing food access p

nutrition programs under threat and state resources stretched thin, counties cannot afford 
to remain passive. By implementing existing food access plans, investing in emergency preparedness, supporting 
food banks, and strengthening kūpuna and keiki feeding programs, counties can make immediate, tangible 
improvements in residents’ daily lives.

At the same time, county action is not a substitute for robust federal and state support. Rather, it is a 
complementary strategy—one that grounds statewide food security goals in the realities of local communities. 
Counties are closest to the people they serve, and that proximity allows them to innovate, partner, and act with 
agility. By seizing these levers, Hawaiʻi’s counties can not only buffer their residents against federal funding 
uncertainty but also build more resilient, equitable food systems for the future.
