 INTRODUCTION: 
A THRIVING HAWAI‘I

HAWAIʻI STANDS AT A CROSSROADS. The path we choose now will define our islands for generations. We can 
either accept a future of diminishing public goods and deepening inequality, or we can choose to build one of 
shared prosperity and collective resilience. 

This choice hinges on a fundamental question of values: who pays for the society we all share? A just future—one 
with quality education, affordable housing, reliable healthcare, and climate-resilient infrastructure—requires a 
fair and adequate investment from all—especially those who have benefitted the most. 

Our current tax code, however, asks less from the wealthy and powerful, leaving working families to shoulder a 

A THRIVING HAWAI‘I • 3

 disproportionate burden and starving our communities of the resources needed to thrive. To build the Hawaiʻi 
we believe in, we must reform our tax system to ensure everyone pays their fair share.

This imperative for equitable and sustainable revenue has become urg

ieve in, we must reform our tax system to ensure everyone pays their fair share.

This imperative for equitable and sustainable revenue has become urgently practical. Due to the 2025 federal 
budget bill, HR1, Hawaiʻi is facing the loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding over the next few 
years. This will leave funding gaps throughout the state budget, especially with Medicaid and SNAP. In addition 
to these cuts, the bill provides $491 million in federal tax cuts to Hawaiʻi’s wealthiest residents. 

These federal cuts come on the heels of Hawaiʻi’s historic income tax cuts that were passed in Act 46, Session 
Laws of Hawaiʻi 2024, which will eventually cost the state over $1 billion a year in tax revenue (see Figure 2).

The state has three options to address these issues: 
•  Cut services;
• 
• 

Issue additional general obligation bonds (pass the costs on to future generations); or
Find other sources of revenue to continue supporting the programs and services that many local residents 
depend on. 

For thousands of Hawaiʻi’s residents, Medicaid and SNAP benefits are a matter of survival. We cannot abandon 
our friends, family, and neighbors who need this support now more than ever. Future generations have already 
been asked to shoulder the consequences of many past decisions. This is a problem we can solve now.

Given that Hawaiʻi’s tax system is regressive (meaning lower-income residents pay a higher effective tax rate than 
higher-income residents),1

Given that Hawaiʻi’s tax system is regressive (meaning lower-income residents pay a higher effective tax rate than 
higher-income residents),1 we recommend legislators balance the state’s upside tax system by asking the wealthy 
and corporations to pay their fair share. 

Doing so is a practical investment in our collective future—a future that should be full of opportunity and success 
for all of Hawaiʻi’s people, not just a privileged few.

 PRESSURE ON 
HAWAI‘I’S BUDGET

Act 46 will place the state budget under significant strain in the years to come. That’s on top of the many critical 
needs facing our communities, all of which need funding to address. Hawaiʻi will be forced to make changes 
to the tax code in order to boost revenue to balance the state budget, and this revenue should come only from 
higher-income households and corporations that can afford to pay more.

ACT 46 CONCERNS

WHILE NEARLY ALL HOUSEHOLDS WILL PAY LESS TAXES AS A RESULT, THE 
LARGEST TAX CUTS WILL GO TO HIGHEST-INCOME HOUSEHOLDS.

At the start of 2024, House Bill 2404 was introduced with the aim of helping Hawaiʻi’s residents with the high cost 
of living by giving them a minor tax break. Each year, it would have slightly adjusted income tax brackets, the 
standard deduction, and personal exemptions to keep up with inflation.

On the last day of the 2024 legislative session, HB2404 was overhauled in Conference Committee with no public 
input or oversight. The vers

On the last day of the 2024 legislative session, HB2404 was overhauled in Conference Committee with no public 
input or oversight. The version that emerged, signed into law as Act 46, makes much larger adjustments to the 
income tax brackets than the version that entered Conference Committee. This means that a larger number of 
high-income households will be taxed at lower rates compared to the original version. 

As an example, the top income bracket for a single filer in 2024 was set at $200,000 and over, with an income tax 
rate of 11 percent. This top 11 percent bracket has already shifted to $325,000 in 2025, and it will rise to $475,000 
in 2029.2

 PROGRESSIVE 
REVENUE PROPOSALS

There are a number of options to raise revenue for Hawaiʻi without adding a financial burden to low- to middle-
income residents. The most straightforward option would be to freeze the income bracket changes in Act 46, 
which would immediately stop the cost of the tax cuts from increasing further (Recommendation 1). 

However, freezing unnecessary tax cuts for the wealthy still leaves us with a tax system in which large 
corporations the richest among us pay less than their fair share. There are many policies at the state’s disposal 
to correct that. These include: taxing capital gains as regular income, creating special taxes on millionaires and 
wealth proceeds, restructuring the conveyance tax, and taxing real estate investment trusts (Recommendation 2).

RECOMMEMDATION 1: FREEZE ACT 46
POTENTIAL REVENUE SAVED: $296 MILLION PER YEAR

Legislators should freeze the implementation of Act 46’s tax bracket changes. This would keep the income 
brackets at their current amounts, while allowing the standard deduction amounts to increase. 

This single action could save at least $296 million in Tax Year 2027—and it would also stop the costs from 
ballooning to $1.4 billion a year beginning in 2032.9 At the same time, it would continue to provide tax relief to 
low- and middle-income households that typically do not itemize

ear beginning in 2032.9 At the same time, it would continue to provide tax relief to 
low- and middle-income households that typically do not itemize their tax returns.

Along with freezing Act 46, Hawaiʻi Appleseed has gathered a list of proven revenue options that would have a 
minimal impact on low- to middle-income taxpayers. All together, these options could raise over $400 million

income from a job. This same person would pay a lower rate of 7.25 percent on their passive income from selling 
stocks. About 68 percent of the capital gains in the state go to people earning over $400,000.11

Capital gains should be taxed at the same rate as ordinary income—ensuring that all taxpayers pay the 
appropriate tax rate on their income, no matter how they earn it.

 OPTION 3: RESTRUCTURING THE CONVEYANCE TAX
Potential Revenue Raised: $68.5 million per year

The Conveyance Tax is a transfer tax paid on the sale of real estate in Hawaiʻi. The current structure of the tax 
can lead to sudden jumps in the amount owed when moving from one bracket to the next (e.g. from the sale of a 
house valued under $1 million versus a house valued above $1 million).

This tax structure could be improved by switching to a marginal rate, similar to income taxes, where only the 
portion above each price threshold is taxed at higher r

re could be improved by switching to a marginal rate, similar to income taxes, where only the 
portion above each price threshold is taxed at higher rates. It could also be improved by increasing the rates on 
luxury homes and second homes.

Restructuring the Conveyance Tax to use marginal rates would actually lower the amount most middle-class 
homeowners would owe upon selling a home. Meanwhile, the owners of high-value homes (many of which live 
out-of-state) would pay more.

Because significant portions of the Conveyance Tax revenue is earmarked for specific funds, much of the 
extra revenue from these changes would go to key priorities like affordable rental housing, transportation 
infrastructure, and the Department of Hawaiian Homelands.

 OPTION 4: TAX REAL ESTATE INVESTMENT TRUSTS
Potential Revenue Raised: $60 million+ per year

A real estate investment trust (REIT) is a company that owns income-generating properties, such as hotels, 
malls and office buildings. People can buy shares in a REIT and earn part of its profits. Examples of REIT-
owned properties include Ala Moana Center, International Marketplace, the Hilton Hawaiian Village, and 
Pearlridge Center.

In 2018, Hawaiʻi’s REITs owned more than $17 billion in real estate and earned roughly $1 billion a year. 12 Since 
REITs do not pay corporate income tax on 90 percent of their profits, Hawaiʻi lost at least $60 million in tax 
revenue in 2018. That figure is likely much higher for 20

rporate income tax on 90 percent of their profits, Hawaiʻi lost at least $60 million in tax 
revenue in 2018. That figure is likely much higher for 2025.13

The majority of REIT shareholders do not live in Hawaiʻi, which means that their income from dividends 
(investments) is not taxed here. As a result, most of the profit earned from commercial properties in Hawaiʻi 
flows out of the state without being taxed.

Closing the REIT tax loophole would ensure these large property owners contribute what they owe to Hawaiʻi’s 
economy. REITs would still keep their federal tax benefits and low local property tax rates, while helping to 
support the local communities their properties depend on.

Potential Revenue Raised: $53.9 million (1% rate)14 per year

The Wealth Proceeds Tax is functions like an expanded capital gains tax—but only for people with very high 
incomes. Most of the tax is paid by millionaires. 

This added 1 percent tax rate would only apply to investment income over $200,000 (single) or $250,000 
(married). Only the wealth proceeds above those amounts is taxed. The tax would apply to income from capital 
gains, dividends, interest, certain business profits, rents, royalties, and some annuity payments

Since wealth proceeds are taxed at the federal level, states can “piggyback” on the existing federal form when 
creating their own wealth proceeds tax.

 CONCLUSION

The choices before us reflect more than a fiscal equation; they are a statement of our values as a community. We 
can continue down the path of a tax system that asks the most from those with the least, while the wealthiest 
contribute less and our public needs go unmet. Or, we can choose a future of shared investment and shared 
prosperity.

The proposals outlined here—from halting the costly Act 46 tax cuts for upper income households, to enacting 
fair taxes on capital gains, luxury properties, and extreme wealth—provide a clear roadmap. They are practical, 
proven policies that ask those who have benefited the most from our economy and society

extreme wealth—provide a clear roadmap. They are practical, 
proven policies that ask those who have benefited the most from our economy and society to finally pay their fair 
share. 

By adopting these measures, we can generate the revenue necessary to protect vital services like Medicaid and 
SNAP, and to invest boldly in housing, education, climate resilience, and the foundations of a thriving Hawaiʻi for 
all. This is how we honor our kuleana to each other and build the resilient, equitable future our islands deserve. 
Let us choose the path of fairness, and fund our shared future together.

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

PUBLIC TRANSIT is more than a way to get from place to place—it’s a tool for growth, opportunity and 
community connection. Transit is particularly important for young people, the largest demographic of residents 
who do not drive. 

When young people can move freely, they gain confidence, independence, and access to the full range of 
opportunities the islands offer. Transit connects keiki to after-school programs, internships, health care, 
recreation and friends, while also building lifelong habits that favor walking, biking and public transportation 
over driving alone.

To improve transit access, localities across the country are increasingly offering reduced and fare-free transit 
programs. This report examines the economic, health, and safety benefits of public transit; summarizes the

1. ECONOMIC BENEFITS

Because 87 percent of all public transit trips directly contribute to the local economy, investment in public transit 
has been shown to spur economic growth.1 The American Public Transportation Association (APTA) reports that 
long-term transit investment yields strong economic benefits, with each $1 billion in additional annual spending 
generating roughly $5 billion in additional GDP over 20 years.2 A $1 billion annual investment in public transit has 
also been found to generate an estimated 17,900 jobs.3 

In 2025, the Ulupono Initiative found that the public cost of the vehicle economy4 in Hawaiʻi was $14,400 
per taxpayer, or $33,600 per household, regardless of vehicle ownership.5 The additional private cost of 
vehicle ownership is substantial—an extra $21,800 per household, per year.6 Given this, it is unsurprising that 
transportation is, on average, the second largest household expenditure in the U.S. In Honolulu, it

The cost of transportation is also regressive, as it consumes a larger share of household budgets for lower-
income residents than for higher-income ones.9 In 2022, the average U.S. household spent 16 percent of their 
after-tax income on transportation, while low-income households in the U.S. spent an average 30 percent of their 
after-tax income on transportation.10 

When individuals shift vehicle trips to transit trips, money saved from vehicle expenditures can be used for 
purchasing power on other necessities, such as housing, food and healthcare. If the U.S. were to sustain a 
higher level of investment in public transit for 20 years, the APTA estimates that would save American drivers an 
estimated $11.7 billion in annual in car operating costs.11

AD SAFETY BENEFITS

Compared to vehicle travel, public transit is safer for its occupants, as well as pedestrians and cyclists. In 2018, a 
study comparing the safety of different roadway users on 10 major urban roads in Montreal found that the injury 
rate for personal vehicle occupants was 3.7 times higher than for bus occupants.18 The researchers found that 
pedestrian injury rates were 4.1 times higher along vehicle-dominated routes compared to bus routes.19 Overall, 
the study estimated that bus travel on these 10 routes alone prevented 2,437 injuries over a 10-year period.20

Local data tells a similar story. In 2024, the City and County of Honolulu’s bus fleet traveled over 21.6 million 
miles.21 That year there was an average of 553,145 miles per major bus collision—roughly 39 major bus collisions 
in total.22 In contrast, the Honolulu Police Department recorded 4,432 major vehicle collisions in 2024.23 

Each year, more than 100 people are killed in crashes on Hawaiʻi’s roads and highways, yet fatal bus crashes 
remain rare.24 From 2012 to 2018, an estimated 12 fatalities were associated with bus collisions.25 These figures 
suggest that shifting trips from personal vehicles to public transit could substantially reduce traffic injuries and 
fatalities, leading to fewer emergency room visits, lower long-term medical costs, and fewer families affected by 
serious crashes.

A. OVERALL RIDERSHIP

While public transit usage differs greatly between Hawaiʻi’s four counties, this section of the report focuses 
primarily on Oʻahu’s TheBus, since this system has the greatest number of riders, and the most data available. 
It is also the state’s most costly transit system. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, average monthly ridership on 
TheBus had decreased by nearly 10 percent between 2015 and 2019 (Figure 3). 27 During the COVID-19 pandemic 
TheBus reached an all-time low of approximately 30.4 million annual rides in 2021.28 

In 2022, annual ridership began to recover, with a 24.9 percent increase in ridership, compared to the dramatic 
decline in 2021. Between 2021 and 2025, total annual

decline in 2021. Between 2021 and 2025, total annual ridership continued to increase by an average of 9 percent

Honolulu’s ongoing fare hikes have likely contributed to its slow post-COVID ridership recovery. TheBus has seen 
two fare increases over the past five years, and in January 2026, the Honolulu City Council voted to pass Bill 
54. This bill will increase fares for adult, youth, and other reduced-fare riders (such as low-income, people with 
disabilities and kūpuna).31 Under Bill 54, both monthly and annual passes for youth will increase by 12.5 percent 
(Figure 4).32 

Increases to transit fares are particularly harmful for low-income riders who rely on it as their primary mode of 
transportation. Based on a 2021–2022 survey conducted by DTS, 21 percent of TheBus riders had a household 
annual income of less than $20,000, and 71 percent had a household income of less than $60,000.33 Su

Increased fares come at a cost. Studies show that when transit fares increase, ridership declines.35 This dynamic

when the prices change.36 In 2019, former DTS Director Wes Frysztacki informed the Honolulu Rate Commission

C. FARES VERSUS OPERATING COSTS

In 2024, the City and County of Honolulu’s public transit system operational costs were an estimated $330 
million.44 During this time period, approximately $47 million in passenger fares were collected, an operating loss 
of approximately $283 million, or an 85 percent deficit. A similar trend occurred in 2022 and 2023, with passenger 
fares covering less than 20 percent of operating costs during those years.45

 LOCAL EXAMPLES

Hawaiʻi County, HI: The Hawaiʻi County Hele-On bus system launched a fare-free pilot program in 2022.46 The 
fare-free program allows anyone to use the bus without a transit pass.47 The program was promoted through the 
Hele-On website, signage on buses, and county press releases.

Following implementation of the fare-free program, in fiscal year (FY) 22 there were over 588,000 passenger rides 
across Hele-On’s buses, vans, and bikeshare services, representing an 81 percent increase from FY21.48 

In 2022, the Hawaiʻi County Council approved the extension of the free fare program through 2025.49 Grant 
funding from the Federal Transit Administration helped to cover the annual fare revenue loss of $560,000.50 
Hawaiʻi County Mass Transit Agency’s acting administrator, Zac Bergum, recently indicated that the agency 
would need to spend over $1 million if the county decided to reintroduce fares and install fare boxes throughout 
the Hele-On system.51

In 2025, the Hawaiʻi County Council approved the extension of the fare-free transit program through 2028.52 Part 
of the reasoning behind its extension has been the continual increase in ridership, which surpassed 940,000 
rides for FY25.53 Ridership now mirrors pre-pandemic le

Hawaiʻi Department of Education: HiDOE has faced an ongoing school bus driver shortage since the onset of 
the COVID-19 pandemic.55 Despite recruitment efforts such as providing signing bonuses, job fairs, and flexible 
schedules for drivers, the shortage has persisted.56

In 2022, HiDOE launched a pilot program called Expanding Ridership to Educate Students in Schools (EXPRESS). 
The EXPRESS program aimed to alleviate the impacts of Hawaiʻi’s school bus driver shortage and improve 
access to school by providing free county bus passes—only be used during the school year—to eligible high 
school students. 

Eligible students must apply through the HiDOE website, and will then receive a transit pass from their respective 
county. In 2022, it was estimated that the DOE spent $3–4 million on the pilot program.57 In 2025, the program 
was expanded to include intermediate school students. 

The program was originally available to all high school students without a school bus pass. However, to be 
eligible for the program currently, students must also live 1.5 miles or further from their school. Students who 
receive a geographic exemption are completely inelig

that many students lack access to school transportation services. However, free transit programs that impose 
seasonal and geographic restrictions limit their impact.

buquerque launched the ABQ Ride Zero Fares pilot, temporarily allowing anyone

Capital Crossroads Special Improvement District, the first fare-free program of its kind to be partially funded by 
downtown property owners.88

 RECOMMENDATIONS

Given the strong evidence that fare-free transit increases ridership, reduces household transportation costs, 
improves access to essential services, and helps build lifelong transit habits, this report recommends that 
Hawaiʻi should enact statewide legislation establishing a permanent, year-round fare-free transit program for all 
residents age 18 and under. 

We acknowledge that affordable transit access is important for all people, and ultimately the most effective 
fare free programs (such as the ones provided by the County of Hawaiʻi and in Albuquerque) provide universal 
transit access. However, providing statewide access for youth is an important step to make this vision a reality. 
Moreover, as demonstrated in this report, young people are the largest demographic of individuals who do not 
drive and are currently underserved by our public transit system—particularly on O

young people are the largest demographic of individuals who do not 
drive and are currently underserved by our public transit system—particularly on Oʻahu. 

Although there is a patchwork of reduced-fare and limited fare-free programs available in Hawaiʻi—including 
the HiDOE’s EXPRESS program and county-specific initiatives—the state still lacks a unified system that 
guarantees all young people equitable access to transportation regardless of county, school type, or family 
income. A statewide program modeled after Washington’s Youth Ride Free initiative would create consistent 
access, reduce administrative burden, and ensure that county transit agencies are financially supported as they 
expand youth ridership.

 KEY COMPONENTS OF A FREE TRANSIT PROGRAM 

1. Provide statewide, zero-fare transit access for youth (18 and under), as well as caregivers accompanying 
young children.

Based on national best practices, youth should be able to ride any county transit system at no cost, and at any 
time of the year. Making the program year-round—not limited to the school year—ensures that young people can 
reliably travel to summer programs, employment, sports, cultural activities, medical care, and family obligations. 

Because guardians may hesitate to allow younger children to travel alone, Hawaiʻi should include a free caregiver 
pass for an adult accompanying youth riders aged 12 or younger.

2. Simple, pass-free boarding to reduce administrative burden

lude a free caregiver 
pass for an adult accompanying youth riders aged 12 or younger.

2. Simple, pass-free boarding to reduce administrative burden and increase transit access.

The statewide program should allow all youth ages 18 and under to board county buses (and the rail on Oʻahu) 
without needing a transit pass, following the proven Washington State model. Eliminating passes removes 
enrollment barriers, shortens boarding times, and significantly reduces administrative costs associated with 
issuing, replacing, and verifying transit passes. National best practices consistently show that fare-free programs 
experience higher utilization and lower overhead when riders are not required to carry specialized transit passes.

To support appropriate fare enforcement while maintaining barrier-free access, bus drivers could ask youth who 
appear older than 18 to show a student ID or state-issued ID. This light-touch identification approach ensures 
program integrity without placing unnecessary burdens on families, schools, or transit agencies. By relying on 
existing IDs rather than creating new pass systems, counties can focus resources on improving service quality 
rather than managing fare administration.

 BACKGROUND

SIGNALIZED INTERSECTIONS are some of the most dangerous places for people walking and biking in Hawaiʻi.1 
These crossings put high volumes of cars and vulnerable road users in direct conflict, often with tragic results. 
Low-cost solutions like Accessible Pedestrian Signals (APS) and Leading Pedestrian Intervals (LPIs) give people a 
safer head start and make crossings more inclusive for those with disabilities. 

While these tools are standard practice in cities across the globe, they are virtually absent in Hawaiʻi. 
With pedestrian injuries and fatalities on the rise, it’s time for lawmakers to require our state and county 
transportation agencies to act.

PEDESTRIAN HEAD START • 3

 ACCESSIBLE PEDESTRIAN SIGNALS (APS)

APS are devices that communicate information 
to blind or low-vision pedestrians about the 
WALK and DON’T WALK intervals at signalized 
intersections in non-visual formats, such as 
audible tones and vibrotactile surfaces. In some 
places, APS also provides audible and Braille 
information about the intersection name and 
crossw

audible tones and vibrotactile surfaces. In some 
places, APS also provides audible and Braille 
information about the intersection name and 
crosswalk orientation.2 

These systems are intended to supplement, but 
not entirely replace, traffic cues.3 For example, 
while the APS can indicate when a person can start 
crossing an intersection, the sound of vehicles is 
still important for blind and low-vision pedestrians 
to know when vehicles are approaching. 

Research shows that APS help pedestrians more 
accurately locate crosswalks and pushbuttons, 
reducing confusion and errors at intersections.4 
They also cut down on delays when beginning 
to cross, allowing people to start during the 
WALK interval with far greater consistency and 
complete crossings before traffic begins to move.5

Broadly speaking, these interventions can 
increase the independence and confidence of 
pedestrians navigating public spaces.6 

While there are reports of these devices being 
used in the U.S. as early as the 1920s—mainly 
near schools for the blind—they were not 
included in the Federal Department of Transportation (DOT) Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) 
until 2000.7

Currently in the U.S., APS systems are typically installed upon request along a specific route of travel for a 
particular individual or group. However, because of stagnant implementation of APS, increasingly class-action 
lawsuits are being brought in major cities on the claims that municipal transportati

use of stagnant implementation of APS, increasingly class-action 
lawsuits are being brought in major cities on the claims that municipal transportation agencies are failing to 
make signaled intersections accessible for visually-impaired pedestrians, as required by the Americans with 
Disability Act (ADA). 

At a minimum, these lawsuits have generally resulted in agreements requiring jurisdictions to establish programs 
for pedestrians to formally request an APS. However, in some localities, these agreements have also required 
municipalities to install APS at existing intersections. For example, in Chicago in 2019, Disability Rights Advocates 
filed a class action lawsuit—later joined by the federal Department of Justice—that challenged Chicago’s 
pedestrian planning practices, which overlooked the safety needs of vision-impaired pedestrians.8 

At the time of the filing, less than 0.5 percent of Chicago’s more than 2,800 signalized intersections provided an 

4 • PEDESTRIAN HEAD START

 APS.9 Following years of litigation, an agreement was reached in 2025 requiring that Chicago equip at least 71 
percent of its signalized intersections with pedestrian signals with APS in the next 10 years.10 The agreement 
also outlines a minimum number of intersections where APS must be installed each year (ranging from 70 to 245 
intersections per year).11

A similar lawsuit and agreement was reached in New York City in 2020, requiring that APS be installed at over 
10,000 intersections

A similar lawsuit and agreement was reached in New York City in 2020, requiring that APS be installed at over 
10,000 intersections over the next 10 years, and that all signalized intersections be equipped with APS within 
15 years.12 

The Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation (HDOT)’s Pedestrian Master Plan and Toolbox discusses APS as an 
important feature to support disabled pedestrians. The plan states that APS should be installed where pedestrian 
push buttons are provided, in accordance with the Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines (PROWAG).13 

The guidelines serve as the technical standard for implementing ADA requirements and mandate that APS be 
installed at any new or modified pedestrian signal.14 Despite this, there is no publicly available information on 
how many intersections in Hawaiʻi have an APS, where intersections with an APS are located, or how pedestrians 
can request that a specific intersection be equipped with an APS. 

LEADING PEDESTRIAN INTERVALS (LPI)

LPIs enable the walk signal to turn on 3–7 seconds early for pedestrians, and in some cases also bicyclists, giving 
them a head-start before motor traffic gets the green.15 LPIs boost pedestrian visibility by providing pedestrians to 
establish their presence in the crosswalk and, in turn, significantly reduces accidents.16

LPIs specifically target one of the most common urban crash types: drivers failing to yield while turning at 
signalized intersections.17 For example,

PIs specifically target one of the most common urban crash types: drivers failing to yield while turning at 
signalized intersections.17 For example, in Seattle about 35 percent of vehicle-pedestrian collisions  at signals 
involve turning vehicles failing to yield.18 

Without an LPI, pedestrians and parallel-turning vehicles receive the “go” signal at the same time, so a driver may 
quickly turn into an intersection and collide with a pedestrian who has just stepped off the curb. As such, LPIs 
are considered a low-cost proven countermeasure by the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) to improve 
pedestrian safety.19 

LPIs particularly help slower-walking pedestrians (such as children, seniors, and those using walkers, wheelchairs 
and other mobility assistance devices) by giving them a protected head start to cross the street. This is particularly 
useful at intersections with poor visibility.20 Transportation agencies often prioritize installing LPIs near schools, 
senior centers and transit hubs to support vulnerable populations.21

Because an LPI lets pedestrians move while parallel traffic is still red, blind or low-vision pedestrians, who use 
the sound of cars as a cue, may miss that early start and step out only after vehicles receive a green light, losing 
the safety benefit that LPIs provide.22 Therefore it is crucial to pair every LPI upgrade with an APS that meets ADA 
requirements. Additionally, transportation agencies often pair LPIs with “No Right Turn on R

ial to pair every LPI upgrade with an APS that meets ADA 
requirements. Additionally, transportation agencies often pair LPIs with “No Right Turn on Red” restrictions to 
better control for conflicts with vehicles turning right.23 

From a behavioral standpoint, LPIs generally do not rely on special user compliance beyond normal signal 
obedience. Pedestrians still cross during the walk signal and drivers still wait for green.24 Some public outreach may 
be helpful to educate road users about the new timing (e.g. signage indicating “Pedestrian Lead Interval in Effect” 
or similar).

 LESSONS FROM 
NATIONAL PROGRAMS

Cities across the nation are implementing LPI and APS systems to improve the safety and accessibility of 
signalized intersections. The section highlights some cities—New York City, Seattle and Los Angeles—that have 
taken steps to implement LPIs city-wide, and the resulting pedestrian safety benefits of these efforts. The 
average cost for installing APS and LPI systems is also discussed in this section. 

BENEFITS

•  New York City: As part of its Vision Zero program, launched in 2014, New York City (NYC) deployed LPIs at 

thousands of intersections. A 2025 Columbia University study analyzing 2,869 LPI-treated intersections in NYC 
found a 33 percent reduction in total pedestrian injuries (fatal and non-fatal) at those sites.25 The effect was 
consistent across different types of intersections.26  

Importantly, fatal vehicle-pedestri

s (fatal and non-fatal) at those sites.25 The effect was 
consistent across different types of intersections.26  

Importantly, fatal vehicle-pedestrian collisions in daytime hours dropped by 65 percent at treated intersections, 
indicating LPIs are especially effective at preventing the most severe collisions.27 NYC’s results underscore that a 
7-second head start can mean the difference between life and death for pedestrians.28

•  Seattle: Seattle began piloting LPIs in 2009 and has since expanded them aggressively as part of the city’s 

Vision Zero strategy.29 At intersections where LPIs were installed from 2009–2018, the city observed a 48 percent 
reduction in collisions involving vehicles failing to yield to pedestrians.30 Furthermore, serious injury and fatal 
pedestrian collisions at those locations declined by 34 percent.31  

As of early 2024, the Seattle Department of Transportation had implemented LPIs at 628 intersections, 

6 • PEDESTRIAN HEAD START

 
 
 representing 64 percent of all of all feasible signalized intersections citywide.32 City officials have made LPIs 
a standard upgrade: Since 2019, Seattle’s policy is to evaluate adding an LPI whenever a signal is built or 
modernized, unless a specific site condition prevents it.33 This proactive, system-wide rollout regularly prevents 
vehicle-pedestrian collisions and has contributed to the success of the city’s Vision Zero program. 

• 

Los Angeles: The Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT) be

sions and has contributed to the success of the city’s Vision Zero program. 

• 

Los Angeles: The Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT) began piloting LPIs in 2014, and has 
since rapidly expanded their implementation.34 Installation of LPIs is focused in downtown and other high-risk 
corridors identified in the city’s Vision Zero Action Plan.35 While LPIs had only been installed at 16 downtown 
intersections in 2016,36 by 2018 there were an estimated 154 intersections with LPIs.37 City leaders noted that 
“pedestrian head-start” signals are a proven way to encourage foot traffic in an urban environment while 
making crossing the street much safer.38  

Along the city’s high-injury network, LADOT continues to retrofit intersections with LPIs, along with other traffic 
calming measures such as reduced speed limits and curb extensions. In 2022, state legislation was enacted to 
require that all newly installed, state-owned traffic signals include the installation, activation and maintenance 
of LPIs, as well as APS.39 In certain areas—such as business, residential and school zones—this requirement also 
applies to state-owned intersections where maintenance work is conducted.40 Subsequently, Assembly Bill 1909 
was passed, allowing bicyclists to use LPIs in California.41

COSTS

One of the major advantages of LPIs is that they can be retrofitted into existing traffic signals relatively easily and 
inexpensively. Unlike physical infrastructure changes, such as curb e

hat they can be retrofitted into existing traffic signals relatively easily and 
inexpensively. Unlike physical infrastructure changes, such as curb extensions or a new traffic signal, an LPI is 
typically a software change to the signal controller timing. 

The FHWA estimates the cost to add an LPI at an intersection ranges from about $200 up to $1,200 per 
intersection.42 The lower end represents cases where only a simple controller setting change is needed, which 
can be done by municipal signal technicians.43 

In some cases, installing LPIs requires conducting a traffic study or installing a new APS device, which require 
additional fiscal resources. However, even the higher end of costs for LPIs is still very low compared to most road 
safety improvements. For example, a City and County of Honolulu official estimated that every mile of sidewalk 
costs approximately $1 million in newer communities with elevated existing curbs and gutters, and closer to $7 
to $10 million per mile in the island’s older communities.44 

The cost of inaction is even greater. Each year, over 100 people are killed in collisions on Hawaiʻi’s roads and 
highways.45 In 2025, there were 129 roadway fatalities in Hawaiʻi, a 20 percent increase from 2024 and the highest 
since 2007.46 Of those fatalities, 38 individuals (29 percent) were pedestrians.47 

Unfortunately this is reflective of the increasing safety threats faced by pedestrians. On Oʻahu the average annual 
number of pedestrian fataliti

7 

Unfortunately this is reflective of the increasing safety threats faced by pedestrians. On Oʻahu the average annual 
number of pedestrian fatalities rose from 15.2 per year during the 2009–2013 time period, to 21 per year during 
the 2014–2018 time period (a 38 percent increase).48

Pedestrian crashes result in the most expensive roadway injuries. The FHWA estimated that every pedestrian 
fatality results in $10.5 million (2019 dollars) of medical care, work loss, household productivity, insurance 
administration and legal costs.49 Even less severe pedestrian injuries can result in an average of $627,462 in 
economic and social costs.50 As such, preventing even one pedestrian injury or fatality easily pays back the 
expense of deploying LPIs, even when installed at a high number of intersections.

 RECOMMENDATIONS 
FOR HAWAI‘I

Pedestrian injuries and fatalities are on the rise in Hawaiʻi. This has had devastating impacts to the individuals 
directly involved in roadway crashes, and has resulted in immense social and economic costs for the greater 
public. There is an urgent need for pedestrian improvements that can be quickly deployed to increase roadway 
safety, and increase the walkability of our island communities. 

This report underscored the benefits of LPIs and APS devices, which are low-cost solutions that improve 
pedestrian safety and accessibility at signalized intersections. Recommendations to deploy these best practices 
in H

low-cost solutions that improve 
pedestrian safety and accessibility at signalized intersections. Recommendations to deploy these best practices 
in Hawaiʻi are provided below. 

1.  Establish a program to request and track LPIs and APS devices. 

The state should require HDOT, in coordination with county transportation agencies, to establish a formal, 
transparent and publicly accessible program to request, evaluate, implement and track LPIs and APS devices at 
signalized intersections. This program would serve as the foundation for a systematic approach to pedestrian 
safety and accessibility, replacing the current ad-hoc and opaque practices that leave many intersections unsafe 
and inaccessible—particularly for blind, low-vision, elderly and mobility-impaired pedestrians.

At present, there is no publicly available information on how many signalized intersections in Hawaiʻi are 
equipped with APS or LPIs, where those intersections are located, or how pedestrians can request these safety 
features. This lack of transparency and formal process not only impedes equitable access to public rights-of-way, 
but also exposes the state and counties to potential legal risk under the ADA. In other jurisdictions, the absence 
of a clear APS request and implementation program has been a central factor in costly class-action litigation, 
resulting in court-mandated timelines and large-scale retrofits. Proactively establishing a program now would 
allow Hawaiʻi to act strategically and

resulting in court-mandated timelines and large-scale retrofits. Proactively establishing a program now would 
allow Hawaiʻi to act strategically and cost-effectively, rather than under court order.

These practices have been employed by some of the agencies highlighted in this report, such as the Seattle 
Department of Transportation, who provides an online map of LPI locations, and statistics on the number of LPIs 
implemented every year. 

2.  Require LPIs and APS at All New and Modified Signalized Intersections

HDOT, as well as the counties, should be required to install LPI and APS devices at all newly-constructed 
signalized intersections, as well as at existing intersections undergoing signal installation, major reconstruction, 
or substantial maintenance work. This policy mirrors California’s Assembly Bill No. 2264, which treats proven 
pedestrian safety treatments as a standard design requirement rather than an optional enhancement.

Embedding LPIs and APS into routine capital and maintenance projects ensures that pedestrian safety 
improvements are implemented systematically and cost-effectively, avoiding the higher costs and delays 

8 • PEDESTRIAN HEAD START

 
 associated with retrofitting intersections after construction. Making these treatments standard practice also 
promotes consistency across jurisdictions and ensures compliance with ADA and PROWAG. 

By institutionalizing LPIs and APS as default features of new and modified intersections, the state can ste

ensures compliance with ADA and PROWAG. 

By institutionalizing LPIs and APS as default features of new and modified intersections, the state can steadily 
expand its pedestrian safety network while ensuring that blind, low-vision, and other vulnerable pedestrians 
benefit equally from signalized crossings.

3.  Require a certain number of LPIs be implemented each year, in tandem with APS devices and other 

safety features. 

In addition to requiring LPIs and APS in new and modified intersections, HDOT and the counties should be 
required to implement a minimum number of LPIs each year at existing signalized intersections, paired with 
APS devices and other complementary pedestrian safety features where appropriate. Establishing an annual 
implementation requirement shifts pedestrian safety from a discretionary activity to a measurable, accountable 
public safety obligation—one that reflects the urgency of rising pedestrian fatalities across the state.

This recommendation calls for HDOT, in coordination with county transportation agencies, to install LPIs 
at a minimum of 20 to 30 signalized intersections per year statewide. Per the guidance of the FHWA,51 when 
considering which intersections should be prioritized for LPI improvements, municipalities should consider the 
following factors: 

•  Crash History: Intersections with multiple crashes or a history of severe injury/fatal pedestrian crashes 

should be considered a priority.

•  Vulnerable Populations: LPIs should

should be considered a priority.

•  Vulnerable Populations: LPIs should also be prioritized where school-aged children, the elderly, disabled, or 

other vulnerable populations are expected to cross.

•  Pedestrian Crossing Volumes: LPIs are useful at intersections with high pedestrian volumes. The estimated 

exposure (product of pedestrian and turning traffic volumes) may be another consideration.

•  One-Way Streets or at T-intersections: Where left-turning vehicles aren’t typically expected to yield to 

oncoming vehicles, LPIs may be useful to increase yielding to pedestrians. 

• 

Intersection Visibility: LPIs may be prioritized where crosswalk visibility is limited or restricted. This could 
include where stopped vehicles, vegetation, or poor lighting decreases visibility. 

Crucially, every new LPI installation should be paired with APS that meets ADA and PROWAG standards. Federal 
guidance and professional consensus make clear that LPIs without APS can unintentionally disadvantage blind 
and low-vision pedestrians, who may miss the early walk interval and lose the intended safety benefit. Pairing 
these treatments ensures equity, legal compliance, and maximum effectiveness. 

Where appropriate, LPIs should also be coordinated with additional safety measures such as “No Turn on 
Red” restrictions, improved crosswalk markings, lighting upgrades, or signal timing adjustments that reflect

Red” restrictions, improved crosswalk markings, lighting upgrades, or signal timing adjustments that reflect 
pedestrian walking speeds.

To support effective implementation, HDOT should be required to publish an annual LPI implementation plan 
identifying candidate intersections, selection criteria, and anticipated timelines. Progress toward the annual 
target should be reported publicly, along with crash and safety performance indicators where available. This 
transparency allows lawmakers and the public to evaluate whether investments are being directed to the 
highest-need locations and whether the program is achieving its intended outcomes.

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

THE CURRENT, MAINSTREAM understanding of how people get around on Oʻahu is largely defined by commuter 
data. However, this data only captures a fraction of our island’s total mobility. This report analyzes the results of 
Hawaiʻi Appleseed’s 2025 Oʻahu Travel Survey, which we used to better understand how residents access school, 
grocery stores, medical appointments, and other destinations that do not fit into the standard 9-to-5 work day.

The survey findings reveal a significant mobility gap. While personal vehicles remain the primary mode to 
access essential and recreational destinations, many households lack access to safe and affordable alternatives. 
Alarmingly, the survey found that: 

•  Half of all residents report that transportation costs negatively impact their ability to reach essential and 

recreational destinations.

•  Nearly 1 in 4 Oʻahu residents faced transportation issues so severe in the past month that they were unable to 

leave their homes.

This report urges decision makers, as w

sidents faced transportation issues so severe in the past month that they were unable to 

leave their homes.

This report urges decision makers, as well as municipal agencies responsible for the planning and design of 
Hawaiʻi roadways, to shift their focus away from vehicle-centered infrastructure and toward transportation 
that puts people first. More specifically, the report’s key recommendations include improving pedestrian 
infrastructure and safety, expanding affordable and reliable transit options, and expanding student 
transportation options.

MOBILITY NEEDS • 3

 LIMITATIONS OF 
COMMUTER DATA

Our most comprehensive data from the U.S. Census has historically only included data on time traveled to work, 
and commuting mode. While 2024 commute mode data shows that 63.7 percent of Oʻahu’s workforce drives 
alone to work, these statistics capture only a fraction of the island’s total mobility (Figure 1).

Census data does provide some insight on how people of different ages, gender, and incomes commute to 
work differently (Figure 2). However, the 2025 Oʻahu Travel Survey moves beyond basic commuter statistics 
to investigate how diverse factors—including geographic region, household income, disability status, age, 
and ethnicity—influence transportation choices for all aspects of daily life. By analyzing these intersecting 
demographics, the survey sought to identify specific mobility gaps and challenges that standard employment-
based data often overlooks.

MOBILITY NEEDS • 13

 Regional Infrastructure Disparity

Perceptions of infrastructure on Oʻahu were starkly different between survey respondents from urban and those 
from rural communities. Respondents from urban areas tended to disagree that there are enough safe sidewalks 
and bike lanes to encourage active transportation, whereas respondents from rural areas tended to disagree that 
there are enough bus routes and stops to support transit usage in their communities. 

Moreover, respondents identifying as Caucasian and those living outside of Urban Honolulu and the Pearl City/
ʻAiea/Moanalua areas were likely to agree that there were enough sidewalks in their community to encourage 
walking. By contrast, residents of Urban Honolulu and those living in households of two or more people were 
more likely to disagree that sidewalk infrastructure in their community was sufficient. 

Regarding bike infrastructure, residents of Urban Honolulu and those identifying as Native Hawaiian/Pacific 
Islander were more likely to disagree that their communities possessed enough safe and accessible bike lanes.

Access to Vehicles

While 85 percent of survey respondents owned at least one personal vehicle, access to vehicles was not a reality

While 85 percent of survey respondents owned at least one personal vehicle, access to vehicles was not a reality 
for all respondents. The survey revealed significant disparities in car ownership exist based on income and 
physical ability. Specifically, those individuals with disabilities or those earning less than $75,000 annually were 
significantly less likely to own a vehicle. Twenty-eight percent of individuals from $75,000 income or below 
households had zero cars at their home, and 30 percent of those with a disability had zero cars at their home.

Among those who did not own a vehicle, the most prevalent barrier to car ownership was inability to afford one, 
which was cited by 29 percent of respondents who did not own a vehicle (Figure 5). Other reasons for a lack 
of individual vehicle ownership included that the respondents were sharing a vehicle with another household 
member or the absence of a valid driver’s license.

 TRANSPORTATION 
INSECURITY ON O‘AHU

Transportation insecurity occurs when barriers such as a lack of vehicle access, unreliable transit, or high costs 
prevent individuals from leaving their home when they need to. This issue is a significant concern across Oʻahu. 
Nearly 1 in 4 respondents reported facing transportation challenges so severe that they were unable to leave 
their homes at some point in the past month (Figure 6). Additionally, 7 percent of respondents reported being 
unable to leave their homes for 15 or more days in the past month because of a problem with transportation.

These mobility gaps are disproportionately felt by specific populations. Respondents living in Pearl City, ʻAiea, 
Moanalua, or Central Oʻahu were more likely to experience high levels of transportation insecurity, compared 
to respondents living in other areas. Transportation insecurity also affected 50 percent of respondents living 
in households with an annual income under $75,000 and 67 percent of respondents with physical or men

disabilities. Additionally, 38 percent of respondents living in households with three or more people, particularly

The financial burden of travel is a primary driver of this trend. Half of all respondents reported that

Survey results indicate that many students would shift to alternative modes of transportation if specific

 RECOMMENDATIONS

The results of the travel survey indicate that current transportation infrastructure and services are not meeting 
the diverse mobility needs of Oʻahu residents. While car dependency is high, residents cite congestion and long 
drive times as their primary concern. 

Yet for many, the alternatives to driving remain insufficient, unsafe, or unaffordable. The significant percentage 
of residents facing transportation insecurity and the willingness of students to use alternative modes highlight 
a clear demand for more safe, affordable, and reliable multimodal options. To improve island-wide mobility, we 
recommend the following policies, targeted to high-need populations.

MOBILITY NEEDS • 19

 1. Improve Pedestrian Infrastructure and Safety

Nearly a third of survey respondents with disabilities indicated that they could not leave their home for 15 or 
more days in the past month due to transportation challenges. To support the 12.9 percent of Oʻahu residents 
living with disabilities, the state and county must prioritize transportation infrastructure that ensures that those 
with physical and mental impairments can move safely and independently throughout their community.3

 Policy efforts should focus on improving the accessibility and safety of transit services, as well as pedestrian 
infrastructure, with a specific emphasis on intersections, which can be among the most dangerous places for 
people who rely on walking or rolling.

Examples of needed improvements which disability rights groups are currently advocating for include leading 
pedestrian intervals and accessible pedestrian signals. These pedestrian improvements give people a safer 
head start and make crossings more inclusive for those with disabilities. Learn more about these low-cost safety 
solutions at https://hiappleseed.org/publications/pedestrian-head-start. 

Sidewalk continuity is also a critical component of a safe and connected pedestrian network. Survey findings 
show that only half of residents feel their communities have sufficient sidewalk infrastructure, and 47 percent of 
students would walk to school if sidewalks were safer and of higher quality.

The state and county should prioritize closing sidewalk gaps, particularly along high-traffic corridors and school 
routes, to ensure that walking is a safe and viable option for all residents.

2. Expand Affordable and Reliable Transit Options

Over half of survey respondents from households earning below $75,000 reported that transportation costs 
regularly prevented them from traveling to essential destinations, or made traveling to essential destinations 
difficult. To address this, the state and county must invest in programs that expand access to public transit and 
active modes of transportation, reducing residents' reliance on and the financial burden of personal vehicle 
ownership altogether.

Improving transit reliability is equally important. Residents cite unreliable and infrequent bus service as a 
significant barrier, even among those willing to use it. Dedicated bus-only lanes on high-traffic corridors would 
reduce travel times, improve schedule reliability, and make public transit a more competitive alternative to 
driving, benefiting riders across all income levels.

While public attention on transportation affordability is often focused on lower fuel taxes, studies show that 
these strategies only provide modest savings for consumers and can further incentivize driving, leading to future 
increased traffic congestion and pollution.4 As shown in Figure 8, investments in the following programs have

households without children to report not being able to leave their home due to transportation issues. Moreover,

services, receiving discounted or free bus passes, improving pedestrian and bike infrastructure, and organizing

urther encourage a shift away from car dependency and build lifelong transit habits, Oʻahu should implement

Summary
Hawaii Wealth Tax Discussion
Daniela and Sarah discussed the potential impact of a wealth proceeds tax in Hawaii, noting that while it wasn't a coalition priority, there was interest from a legislator to introduce it. They acknowledged the need to gather more data on how this tax would specifically affect Hawaii. Devin, an expert on capital gains tax, was expected to join the meeting to provide insights into the legislative statu

uld specifically affect Hawaii. Devin, an expert on capital gains tax, was expected to join the meeting to provide insights into the legislative status and nuances of the tax.
Hawaii Capital Gains Tax Proposals
The meeting focused on discussing two tax proposals: the capital gains tax and the wealth proceeds tax. Devin presented an overview of the capital gains tax, explaining that it currently has a preferential rate of 7.25% in Hawaii and primarily benefits the wealthy. He outlined two potential proposals: taxing capital gains at the same rate as ordinary income, which could raise $85 million, or increasing the rate to 9% to raise $44 million. The group discussed opposition to closing the capital gains loophole, with arguments centering on punishing successful investments and affecting small business investment. Messaging Guide
A Fair Tax System to Fund Hawaiʻi’s Future


3 Topline Messages
1. Goods for the Common Good 
Taxes pay for things that help our communities thrive, like housing, healthcare, food security, roads, schools, and care for our keiki and kupuna. Our local businesses rely on these investments to p

hrive, like housing, healthcare, food security, roads, schools, and care for our keiki and kupuna. Our local businesses rely on these investments to produce a healthy and educated workforce they need to succeed. These investments are the building blocks of a healthy, thriving community and we deserve to have the very best.  Fair taxation is how we’ll get there.


2. Everyone Pays Their Fair Share
Tax fairness means those with more pay more. A tax system that ensures everyone pays what they can afford—especially those who have benefited most from Hawai‘i’s land, resources, and public infrastructure - ensures a resilient local economy. Asking those with over $1M household income to pay their fair share is not only responsible–it’s smart. The ultra-wealthy will still be wealthy, even if their taxes go up a couple of percentage points. 


3. The Choice is Clear, and the Time is Now
Federal cuts to critical safety net programs, an affordability crisis, and the growing threat of climate change mean that the State could be facing an unprecedented budget shortfall that cannot simply be ignored. Our policymakers have 3 very clear choices:  
   1. Austerity: Cut education programs and public services, putting an even larger strain on already struggling families and community resources
   2. Issue bonds: This is essentially using the State’s “credit card,” passing more debt on to future generations.
   3. Apply taxes fairly to grow the middle class, support the needs of our communities,

’s “credit card,” passing more debt on to future generations.

Who We Are
The Hawaiʻi Tax Fairness Coalition is a statewide alliance of nonprofits, community organizations, unions, advocates, researchers, and service providers working to create a more equitable tax system—one that raises the revenue our state n

nizations, unions, advocates, researchers, and service providers working to create a more equitable tax system—one that raises the revenue our state needs without placing the burden on low- and moderate-income families.
We advocate for practical, achievable reforms that ensure those who benefit most from Hawaiʻi’s economy contribute fairly so the state can sustainably fund housing, healthcare, education, infrastructure, and essential community services.
________________


A Fair Tax System: The “Why” and the “How”
A fair tax system isn’t just good economic policy—it’s foundational to a healthy democracy.
* Funds essential services. It ensures Hawaiʻi can sustain strong public services and safety-net programs, which are the backbone of stable democracies worldwide.
* Builds public trust. People lose faith in government when they see loopholes for the wealthy or when working families carry more than their share. Fair taxation shows that the rules apply evenly, strengthening confidence in our institutions.
* Balances political power. When wealth is overly concentrated, a small group can exert outsized influence over policy and elections. We’re seeing this play out now with federal cuts to essential programs like SNAP and Medicaid—decisions that don’t reflect the needs of most people.
So how do we get there? Our Core Policy Priorities
A fair tax system is one where the wealth gap shrinks after taxes are paid—not grows. But in Hawaiʻi, the opposite is happening: the wealthiest pay

es
A fair tax system is one where the wealth gap shrinks after taxes are paid—not grows. But in Hawaiʻi, the opposite is happening: the wealthiest pay a smaller share of their income than those with the least, widening the gap every year. To fix this, we pursue two main strategies: 
1. Raise Revenue to Support Critical Services. In 2026, especially after recent federal cuts, our top priority is restoring sustainable state revenue by:
* Modernizing the Income Tax: Freeze the income tax cuts passed in 2024. Restore higher marginal rates for top earners.
* Closing the Capital Gains Loophole: Tax investment income the same as wages.
* Reforming Property & Real Estate Taxes: Increase conveyance tax rates on luxury and investment properties, and ensure Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) contribute appropriately.
2. Strengthen Credits for Working Families. Our coalition also supports expanding refundable credits—like the EITC, child credits, dependent care credits, and the food excise tax credit—to boost take-home income for low- and moderate-income households.

upport immediately upon reentry. Food insecurity disproportionately affects people returning from incarceration, who face barriers to employment, housing, and benefits access. le to more people, thereby alleviating hunger and preventing long-term health issues like diabetes, heart disease, stroke, and depression.[1]

Dear Chair Matayoshi, Vice Chair Grandinetti, and Members of the Committee,


Thank you for the opportunity to present testimony in strong support of HB2367. This bill closes a critical gap in our pay transparency law by requiring all employers—regardless of size—to disclose salary ranges in job listings. It is a data-driven, structural reform that addresses entrenched wage disparities and advances economic justice for Hawaiʻi's workers and families.


The Wage Gap in Hawaiʻi: Stubborn and Costly


Despite progress in recent decades, significant wage disparities persist in Hawaiʻi. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Hawaiʻi women had median usual weekly earnings of $797 in 2018, or just 82.6 percent of the $965 median earnings of their male counterparts.[1] In 2023, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported women in Hawaiʻi earned 82.4 percent of what men earned ($902 vs. $1,095).[2] For 2024, updated estimates place the ratio at approximately 87 percent ($987 for women vs. $1,138 for men).[3]


This is not simply a plateau; it is a backslide. Hawaiʻi wome

es place the ratio at approximately 87 percent ($987 for women vs. $1,138 for men).[3]


This is not simply a plateau; it is a backslide. Hawaiʻi women's earnings relative to men peaked at 92.8 percent in 2014 and have since fallen by more than five percentage points.[4] Whatever progress we thought we were making is anything but consistent, and wage opacity is a significant part of the problem.


The Human and Economic Costs Are Staggering


These disparities are not abstract numbers; they represent real dollars stolen from families who can least afford to lose them. Our analysis of what equal pay would mean for Hawaiʻi's working women reveals profound impacts:
* Poverty reduction: If women earned the same pay as comparable men, the poverty rate among working women in Hawaiʻi would decrease by more than half—from 5.4 percent to just 2.5 percent.[5]
* Single mothers: The poverty rate for families headed by working single mothers would drop by close to half, from 21.3 percent to 10.7 percent.[6]
* Working mothers: More than 61 percent of working mothers would see increased earnings.[7]
* Children: The poverty rate among children of working mothers would fall by more than half, from 10.9 percent to 4.5 percent.[8]


These are not marginal improvements. They are transformative changes that would lift thousands of Hawaiʻi families out of poverty, reduce reliance on public assistance, and strengthen the economic security of communities across the state.

Why Transparency Matters


Pay transparency is a proven mechanism for addressing wage disparities. When compensation is hidden, disparities can persist unnoticed and unchallenged. Workers negotiating in the dark cannot know whether they are being offered fair wages. Women and people of color, who have historically been disadvantaged in wage negotiations, are disproportionately harmed by this information asymmetry.


HB2367 addresses this by requiring all employers to disclose salary ranges in job listings. This simple requirement:
* Empowers workers with information they need to negotiate from a position of knowledge.
* Exposes disparities that might otherwise remain hidden.
* Creates accountability for employers to justify their compensation practices.
* Accelerates progress toward closing wage gaps.


Closing the Exemption Gap


Current law exempts employers with fewer than 50 employees from salary range disclosure requirements. This exemption is not justified by evidence or equity. HB2367 removes this exemption, ensuring that every job seeker in Hawaiʻi—regardless of where they apply—can see compensation upfront.

The evidence from those states shows that transparency laws narrow wage gaps, improve worker mobility, and strengthen labor market function.

We believe this policy is a fair and targeted way to raise substantial revenue from the very wealthiest residents, while protecting low- and middle-income families and helping to address our state’s deep inequities.
Why Hawaiʻi needs a wealth proceeds tax
Hawaiʻi has one of the highest costs of living in the nation, and many families are struggling to keep up with housing, food, and other basic needs. At the same time, a small number of ultra‑wealthy households hold a disproportionate share of assets and investment gains. A wealth proceeds tax would ensure that a portion of these very large asset gains is taxed so that those at the top contribute more in line with their ability to pay.​
This approach shifts part of the tax burden away from workers and consumers and toward large concentrations of wealth, allowing the state to fund essential services without raising broad-based taxes.​
How the wealth proceeds tax works
Under the proposal, Hawaiʻi would levy a tax on very large “wealth proceeds” — significant gains from assets such as stocks, closely held businesses, or other high‑value investments — once those gains exceed a high threshold.​
Key design elements include:
* The tax applies only to extremely large one‑time or occasional gains, well above

those gains exceed a high threshold.​

* Retirement accounts and modest asset sales would not be affected because the threshold is set high enough that only the ultra‑rich would pay.​
Because of this design, the tax would fall overwhelmingly on the top fraction of 1% of Hawaiʻi residents, leaving the vast majority of households untouched.​
Revenue and equity impact
A wealth proceeds tax structured in this way is projected to raise hundreds of millions of dollars over time, with the annual amount depending on market conditions and the number of very large asset sales in a given year.​

* This helps reduce the upside‑down nature of Hawaiʻi’s tax system, in which low‑ and middle‑income households currently pay a higher share of their income in state and local taxes than the richest residents.​
By directing this new revenue toward housing, education, health care, and climate resilience, Hawaiʻi can make meaningful progress on its most pressing challenges while narrowing wealth and racial inequities.​

I support keeping tax relief for families who need it, but high-income earners should not receive tax cuts. Why this matters
Federal spending cuts will put the state’s programs and services at risk, including Medicaid and SNAP. Many of Hawaiʻi’s families depend on these safety nets to make ends meet.
Act 46 raises the standard deduction and widens the income tax brackets over several years—which means that many taxpayers will be taxed at lower rates. Unfortunately, these tax cuts will cost the state around $240 million in the first year, and this cost will grow over time. When they are fully phased in around 2031, the tax cuts will cost over $1.4 billion a year, which is roughly a tenth of general fund tax revenues. 
This will shrink the budget we use to fund core programs. Because federal dollars are uncertain, losing this much state revenue makes it harder to keep services running when communities need them most.
Who benefits most
Most households will get a tax cut, but the largest cuts go to the highest‑income taxpayers. This tilt toward high earners grows as the law phases in, increasing the long-term cost to the state budget.
